cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Search Engine Optimization: The process of improving a website to increase its visibility in organic search engine results.
cards.example: Optimizing blog post headers and meta descriptions to rank higher on Google for "best running shoes".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: SEM: Search Engine Marketing. Marketing a business on search engines. In everyday usage it means paid ads on search results pages (Google Ads); in the broad sense, SEM = SEO + SEA (paid search).
cards.example: Running a Google Ads campaign to appear at the very top of the page for "digital marketing agency".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Click-Through Rate: The percentage of people who clicked on an ad or link after seeing it. Formula: (Clicks / Impressions) * 100.
cards.example: An ad with 1,000 impressions and 20 clicks has a CTR of 2%.
cards.cloze: Click-Through Rate: The percentage of people who clicked on an ad or link after seeing it. Formula: {{c1::(Clicks / Impressions) * 100}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Call to Action: A prompt on a website or ad that tells the user to take a specific action.
cards.example: A bright orange button on a landing page that says "Download Your Free E-book Now".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Cost Per Click: The actual price you pay for each click in your pay-per-click (PPC) marketing campaigns.
cards.example: Paying $0.50 every time someone clicks on your Facebook sponsored post.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Cost Per Acquisition: The average cost of one defined conversion (sale, lead, sign-up) on a given campaign or channel. Formula: Ad spend / Number of conversions.
cards.example: If you spend $100 on ads and get 5 sales, your CPA is $20.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Return on Investment: A measure used to evaluate the efficiency of an investment. Formula: (Net Profit / Cost of Investment) * 100.
cards.example: Spending $1,000 on a campaign that brings in $3,000, i.e. $2,000 of net profit, gives a 200% ROI.
cards.cloze: Return on Investment: A measure used to evaluate the efficiency of an investment. Formula: {{c1::(Net Profit / Cost of Investment) * 100}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Key Performance Indicator: A measurable value that demonstrates how effectively a company is achieving key business objectives.
cards.example: A Social Media Manager tracking "Monthly Follower Growth" as a primary success metric.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A standalone web page, created specifically for a marketing or advertising campaign, where a visitor "lands" after clicking a link.
cards.example: A dedicated page for a webinar registration with no distracting navigation links.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: In the classic sense (Universal Analytics, Matomo): the percentage of single-page sessions, where the visitor leaves without viewing anything else. GA4 uses a different, engagement-based definition.
cards.example: A high bounce rate on a product page might mean the content doesn't match what the ad promised.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of users who take a desired action (like a purchase or signup). Formula: (Conversions / Total Visitors) * 100.
cards.example: If 100 people visit your site and 3 buy something, your conversion rate is 3%.
cards.cloze: The percentage of users who take a desired action (like a purchase or signup). Formula: {{c1::(Conversions / Total Visitors) * 100}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Software as a Service: A software licensing and delivery model in which software is licensed on a subscription basis.
cards.example: Using tools like Canva, Slack, or HubSpot via a monthly paid subscription.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of customers or subscribers who stop communicating or purchasing from a business during a given time period.
cards.example: A streaming service losing 5% of its subscribers every month.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An inbound link: a link placed on a third-party site that points to your site. From your site's point of view it is a received link, one of Google's main popularity signals.
cards.example: A tech blog linking to your startup's website: you receive a backlink that strengthens your site's credibility in Google's eyes.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Moz's 0 to 100 score estimating how well a domain can rank on Google based on its link profile. A comparative prediction, not a signal Google uses.
cards.example: A link from the New York Times (Moz DA close to 95) is worth more than a link from a brand new personal blog (DA 5).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Search Engine Results Page: The page displayed by a search engine in response to a query by a user.
cards.example: Trying to get your product featured in the "People Also Ask" section of the Google SERP.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The total number of times your content or ad is displayed, regardless of whether it was clicked or not.
cards.example: Your Instagram post displayed 500 times during the day, including several times to the same user: 500 impressions.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The total number of unique people who see your content.
cards.example: If 1 user sees your ad 5 times, your Reach is 1, but your Impressions are 5.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Metric that divides the interactions a piece of content receives (likes, comments, shares, saves) by a reference base: followers, reach or impressions depending on the platform and tool. The per-follower version is used to compare accounts.
cards.example: Calculating the ratio of Likes, Comments, and Shares relative to your total followers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A person or business who has shown interest in your product or service in some way, shape, or form.
cards.example: Someone who fills out a "Contact Us" form on your website to get a quote.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A funnel-shaped model that breaks the path to purchase into stages (awareness, consideration, conversion), with fewer people remaining at each level.
cards.example: Awareness (Top), Consideration (Middle), and Conversion (Bottom).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Top of the Funnel: The first stage of the buyer's journey where the goal is to create awareness.
cards.example: A viral TikTok video or an educational blog post aimed at people who don't know your brand yet.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Middle of the Funnel: The stage where leads are evaluating your company and learning more about your products.
cards.example: Sending a case study or a comparison guide to someone who signed up for your newsletter.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Bottom of the Funnel: The final stage where leads are ready to make a purchase decision.
cards.example: Offering a "15-minute free consultation" or a "limited time discount code" to close the sale.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Pay-Per-Click: An internet advertising model used to drive traffic to websites, in which an advertiser pays a publisher when the ad is clicked.
cards.example: Running ads on Bing where you only pay when a user actually enters your site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Visitors who land on your website as a result of unpaid search results.
cards.example: A user searching for "healthy recipes" and clicking on your blog without it being a "Sponsored" link.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Any traffic that comes to your website from a paid advertisement.
cards.example: Users arriving at your site via Facebook Ads, YouTube Ads, or Google Search Ads.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The act of sending a commercial message, typically to a group of people, using email.
cards.example: Sending a weekly newsletter to your subscribers with the latest AI news.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of delivered emails that were opened. An unreliable metric since 2021: Apple Mail Privacy Protection preloads images and registers opens that never happened.
cards.example: Having an open rate of 25% on your latest promotional email blast.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of recipients who clicked at least one link in your email, out of the number of emails delivered (bounces excluded). Not to be confused with click-to-open rate (CTOR).
cards.example: Tracking how many people clicked the "Buy Now" link inside your newsletter.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A randomized experimentation process wherein two or more versions of a variable are shown to different segments of website visitors.
cards.example: Testing a "Red Button" vs a "Green Button" to see which one gets more clicks.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Content Management System: software that lets you create, edit and publish a site's content without coding, and that also renders it for visitors (themes, pages), such as WordPress.
cards.example: Using WordPress, Shopify, or Webflow to build and update your website.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Uniform Resource Locator: The address of a given unique resource on the Web.
cards.example: https://www.google.com is a URL.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Alternative Text: The alt attribute of an img tag that describes the image for screen readers, search engines, and display when the image fails to load.
cards.example: Setting alt="Man playing badminton" on the img tag so a screen reader can describe the photo and Google understands what it shows.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An HTML element that provides a brief summary of a web page for search engines and users.
cards.example: The 160-character snippet under the title in Google search results.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The visible, clickable text in a hyperlink.
cards.example: In the sentence "Click here for our pricing," the words "Click here" are the anchor text.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A form of social media marketing involving endorsements and product placement from influencers.
cards.example: A fitness coach promoting a specific protein powder on their Instagram Story.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A marketing arrangement by which an online retailer pays a commission to an external website for traffic or sales generated from its referrals.
cards.example: Using a custom link in a YouTube description to earn a 10% commission on every sale.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advertising approach where paid ads adopt the look, tone, and function of the medium that carries them, so they don't interrupt the experience. Refers to the practice as a whole.
cards.example: A "Sponsored Content" article on a news site that looks just like a regular news story.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: User Experience: The overall experience of a person using a product such as a website or computer application.
cards.example: Ensuring a website is easy to navigate and loads quickly on mobile phones.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: User Interface: The series of screens, pages, and visual elements (like buttons and icons) that enable a person to interact with a product.
cards.example: Designing the specific colors, fonts, and layout of a mobile app.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The full set of interactions and experiences a customer actually has with your brand across every touchpoint, before, during and after the purchase.
cards.example: A user seeing a LinkedIn post, then visiting the site, then receiving an email, then buying.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The share of consumers who can recognize or name a brand, measured by survey. It tells whether the brand is known, not whether it comes to mind at the moment of purchase (that is salience).
cards.example: Recognizing the Apple logo or the Nike "Swoosh" immediately without seeing the name.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Visitors who arrive on your site by clicking a link placed on another website, excluding search engines and social networks (which GA4 groups separately).
cards.example: Traffic coming from a mention of your blog on a Wikipedia page.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Visitors who arrive on your site with no identifiable source (no referrer): a URL typed into the browser, a bookmark, or a link opened from an app or a document.
cards.example: A fan of your newsletter typing "theopezet.com" directly into Chrome.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A graphical representation of data where values are depicted by color, showing where users click or scroll on a page.
cards.example: Using Hotjar to see that most users never scroll past the first half of your landing page.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of gathering information relevant to a particular topic or area of interest and sharing it.
cards.example: A newsletter that summarizes the 5 best AI news of the week for its readers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Content that remains perpetually relevant and "fresh" for readers over a long period of time.
cards.example: A guide on "How to play Badminton" is evergreen, while "2024 Olympic Results" is not.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The umbrella term for reaching, with ads, people who have already visited your site or used your app, whatever the format or platform.
cards.example: Showing a Facebook ad for a pair of shoes to a user who added them to their cart but didn't buy.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A sub-group of your audience that shares certain characteristics (age, location, interests).
cards.example: Creating an email list specifically for "Customers who haven't bought in 6 months".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Customer Relationship Management: Technology for managing all your company’s relationships and interactions with customers and potential customers.
cards.example: Using HubSpot to track every conversation your sales team has with a lead.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A site map: a page or file listing a site's pages and how they are organized. It can be HTML, for visitors, or XML, for search engine bots.
cards.example: A "Site map" page in the footer that lists every section to help visitors (and bots) find their way around.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The release of a new product or service to a restricted audience or market before the full launch.
cards.example: Opening your new online store only to your 50 most loyal followers to test for bugs.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A style of promotion that relies on the audience itself to spread the message of a product or service, mainly through sharing.
cards.example: The "Ice Bucket Challenge" which spread rapidly across social media through user sharing.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Consumers spontaneously recommending a brand or product to each other in their own conversations. Word-of-mouth marketing tries to trigger and amplify it.
cards.example: A happy customer telling their friend "You have to try this new coaching program!".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An incentive that marketers offer to potential buyers in exchange for their email address or other contact information.
cards.example: A "Free PDF Checklist for SEO" offered at the end of a blog post.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A permanent delivery failure: the email is rejected because the recipient's address is invalid, non-existent or its domain no longer exists. The address must be removed from the list immediately.
cards.example: Sending an email to a misspelled address like "test@gmailll.com".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A temporary delivery failure: the email reached the recipient's mail server but was refused for now, often because the inbox is full or the server is down. The send can be retried.
cards.example: A temporary delivery failure because the user's mailbox has no space left.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of people who opt-out of your email list after receiving an email.
cards.example: A high unsubscribe rate (over 1%) usually means your content isn't relevant to your audience.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Statistical data relating to the population and particular groups within it (Age, Gender, Income).
cards.example: Targeting "Males, aged 18-35, living in Paris" for a football-related product.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The study of consumers based on their activities, interests, and opinions (Values, Lifestyle).
cards.example: Targeting people who "Value sustainable fashion and enjoy hiking on weekends".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: User-Generated Content: Any form of content, such as images or videos, that was created by consumers rather than brands.
cards.example: A customer posting a video of themselves unboxing your product on TikTok.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The interaction between a consumer and a brand (likes, comments, shares, saves).
cards.example: High engagement on a LinkedIn post suggests the topic is highly relevant to your network.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A set of rules or calculations used by social media platforms or search engines to determine what content users see.
cards.example: The LinkedIn algorithm prioritizing posts that get a lot of comments in the first hour.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The psychological phenomenon where people copy the actions of others to decide how to behave in a given situation.
cards.example: Displaying "Join 10,000+ subscribers" on your newsletter signup form.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The small icon that appears next to the website title in a browser tab.
cards.example: The small multicoloured "G" icon you see in your tab when you are on Google.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A link on a website that no longer works, usually because the page has been moved or deleted.
cards.example: Clicking a link and landing on a "404 Not Found" error page because the article was deleted.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The standard HTTP response code indicating that the client was able to communicate with a given server, but the server could not find what was requested.
cards.example: A user typing a wrong URL on your site and seeing a "Page not found" message.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A variation of a CTA that focuses on the benefit the user will receive rather than the action they take.
cards.example: Using "Start growing my business" instead of just "Submit".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The act or occupation of writing text for the purpose of advertising or other forms of marketing.
cards.example: Writing the persuasive text for a Facebook ad to convince people to buy.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategic marketing approach focused on creating and distributing valuable, relevant, and consistent content to attract an audience.
cards.example: Writing helpful blog posts about fitness to eventually sell coaching services.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Visitors who access your website via a desktop computer or laptop.
cards.example: Analyzing if your B2B software is mostly used on desktop rather than mobile.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Visitors who access your website via a smartphone or tablet.
cards.example: Optimizing your site for mobile because 80% of your users come from Instagram.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of loading a webpage with keywords in an attempt to manipulate a site's ranking in Google search results.
cards.example: A bad SEO practice: "We sell the best footballs. Our footballs are cheap footballs. Buy footballs here."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A more specific (and often longer) search phrase that has lower search volume but higher conversion value.
cards.example: "Best red badminton racket for beginners" instead of just "Racket".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The specific group of consumers most likely to want your product or service.
cards.example: Focusing your marketing on "Students interested in digital marketing".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The use of optimization strategies, techniques, and tactics that focus on a human audience and completely follow search engine rules.
cards.example: Focusing on high-quality content and natural link building.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The use of aggressive SEO strategies that focus only on search engines and usually do not obey search engine guidelines.
cards.example: Using "hidden text" or "link farms" to trick Google's algorithm.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Unsolicited, usually commercial, messages sent to a large number of recipients.
cards.example: Irrelevant comments on a blog post or junk emails in your inbox.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The use of software to automate marketing activities such as email marketing, social media posting, and ad campaigns.
cards.example: Setting up an email to be sent automatically 24 hours after someone leaves their cart.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A program that automatically runs repetitive tasks over the Internet (crawling pages, clicking, posting), often imitating a human, without necessarily holding a conversation.
cards.example: Googlebot, the Google crawler that visits your pages to index them, or fake bot clicks that inflate your analytics.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A small text file the browser stores on the user's device at a website's request, so the site can recognize them from one page or visit to the next (session, preferences, tracking).
cards.example: Using cookies to remember what items a user put in their shopping cart.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statement or legal document that discloses some or all of the ways a party gathers, uses, discloses, and manages a customer or client's data.
cards.example: A mandatory page on your site explaining how you handle user emails (GDPR).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: General Data Protection Regulation: A regulation in EU law on data protection and privacy.
cards.example: Asking for explicit consent before tracking a user's behavior on your website.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique for drawing customers to products and services via content marketing, social media marketing, and SEO.
cards.example: Attracting leads by providing helpful YouTube tutorials about marketing tools.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A traditional method of marketing where a company initiates the conversation and sends its message out to an audience.
cards.example: Cold calling, TV commercials, or mass email blasts to people who didn't ask for them.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Assigning points to each lead based on profile and behavior to estimate how likely they are to buy, so sales can prioritize which leads to contact first.
cards.example: Giving a lead +10 points for downloading a guide and +50 for requesting a demo.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An individual who has the power to affect purchase decisions of others because of their authority, knowledge, or relationship with their audience.
cards.example: A LinkedIn creator who talks about AI and is trusted by their followers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The commercial value that derives from consumer perception of the brand name of a particular product, rather than from the product itself.
cards.example: People being willing to pay $1000 for a phone just because it has an Apple logo.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Unique Selling Proposition: The one specific advantage that sets you apart from every competitor, summed up in a short promise.
cards.example: "Fresh hot pizza delivered in 30 minutes or it's free." (Domino's).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The ability of a business or system to grow and manage increased demand without compromising performance.
cards.example: An online course is highly scalable because you record it once and sell it to millions.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A semi-fictional representation of your ideal customer based on market research and real data.
cards.example: "Marketing Manager Marc, 35, lives in London, struggles with tracking ROI.".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An audio show (sometimes also video) released in regular episodes, distributed via RSS feed on platforms such as Spotify or Apple Podcasts, and listened to on demand, by streaming or download.
cards.example: Creating a weekly 20-minute audio show about US Rap for fans.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A small image used to represent a larger image or a video, designed to catch the eye.
cards.example: The custom image you see on a YouTube video before you click "Play".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A blog kept in video form: the creator regularly films and publishes episodes about their daily life or a specific topic, most often on YouTube, speaking directly to the camera.
cards.example: A "Day in the life of a digital marketing intern" video on YouTube.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A digital book, in marketing usually a PDF of a few dozen pages that covers a topic in depth. It mostly serves as a lead magnet: offered as a download in exchange for an email address.
cards.example: Offering a "Guide to Investing in S&P 500" as a free PDF download.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A seminar or training session broadcast live over the internet (Zoom, Livestorm), with prior registration and real-time interaction (questions, polls). Often used to generate B2B leads.
cards.example: Hosting a live 1-hour training session on how to use AI for marketing.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Lifetime Value: The total revenue a business can expect from a single customer over the whole business relationship. Formula: Average Purchase Value * Purchases per Year * Customer Lifespan in Years.
cards.example: A gym member paying $50/month for 3 years has an LTV of $1,800.
cards.cloze: Lifetime Value: The total revenue a business can expect from a single customer over the whole business relationship. Formula: {{c1::Average Purchase Value * Purchases per Year * Customer Lifespan in Years}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Customer Acquisition Cost: The average cost of winning one new customer. Formula: (Marketing Spend + Sales Spend) / Number of New Customers.
cards.example: If you spend $5,000 to get 100 customers, your CAC is $50.
cards.cloze: Customer Acquisition Cost: The average cost of winning one new customer. Formula: {{c1::(Marketing Spend + Sales Spend) / Number of New Customers}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Return on Ad Spend: A marketing metric that measures the amount of revenue a business earns for each dollar it spends on advertising. Formula: (Revenue from Ads / Cost of Ads).
cards.example: Earning $5 for every $1 spent on Google Ads results in a ROAS of 5.0 (or 500%).
cards.cloze: Return on Ad Spend: A marketing metric that measures the amount of revenue a business earns for each dollar it spends on advertising. Formula: {{c1::(Revenue from Ads / Cost of Ads)}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The rule, or set of rules, that determines how credit for sales and conversions is assigned to touchpoints in conversion paths.
cards.example: Using "Last Click" attribution gives 100% of the credit to the final ad seen before the purchase.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A small step taken by a user on your website that indicates they are moving towards a main conversion.
cards.example: A user signing up for a newsletter or adding a product to a "Wishlist" without buying yet.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The primary goal of a website, such as a completed purchase or a signed contract.
cards.example: A user completing the checkout process for a $200 order on an e-commerce site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of dividing a customer base into groups of individuals that are similar in specific ways relevant to marketing.
cards.example: Grouping customers by "High Spenders," "Discount Seekers," and "Inactive Users".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A growth marketing framework representing the five stages of a customer's journey: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue.
cards.example: Using the Pirate Metrics to identify that your app has great acquisition but very low retention.
cards.cloze: A growth marketing framework representing the five stages of a customer's journey: {{c1::Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The "Aha! moment" when a user first realizes the value of your product.
cards.example: A new Slack user sending their first message to a teammate.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The ability of a company to turn customers into repeat buyers and prevent them from switching to a competitor.
cards.example: A subscription box service focusing on keeping customers subscribed for at least 12 months.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When a customer recommends your product to their network, often incentivized by a reward.
cards.example: Dropbox giving extra storage space to users who invite their friends to sign up.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A study over time of the behavior of a group of users who share a common characteristic, most often their sign-up or first-purchase date (acquisition cohort).
cards.example: Tracking if users who joined in January spend more than users who joined in June.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The use of data and analytics to identify which customers are most likely to stop using a service.
cards.example: A telecom company noticing a user has stopped using data and offering them a discount before they leave.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The use of software to automate repetitive marketing tasks such as email, social media, and website actions.
cards.example: An automated "Welcome Sequence" of 5 emails sent over 10 days to every new subscriber.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Keeping a relationship going with leads who are not ready to buy yet (emails, helpful content) at every stage of the funnel, until they are ripe for a sale.
cards.example: Sending helpful educational content to a lead who downloaded a whitepaper to keep your brand top-of-mind.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A marketing funnel that runs automatically 24/7/365 without the need for manual intervention.
cards.example: A webinar funnel that users can enter and complete at any time of the year.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of monitoring social media channels for mentions of your brand, competitors, product, and related keywords.
cards.example: A brand tracking the hashtag #Badminton to see what players are complaining about regarding their rackets.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The unique space a brand occupies in the minds of the customers in its target market.
cards.example: Volvo positioning itself as the "safest" car brand in the world.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statement summing up the full set of benefits a customer gets from your product or service and why they should choose it. Broader than a USP, which keeps a single differentiator.
cards.example: "The easiest way to build a professional website in under 10 minutes.".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Web or email content that changes based on the behavior, preferences, and interests of the user.
cards.example: An email showing winter coats to users in London and t-shirts to users in Miami.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The act of tailoring a service or a product to accommodate specific individuals.
cards.example: An app greeting you with "Hello Théo" and suggesting songs based on your past listens.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An audience created by an ad platform that shares similar characteristics with your existing customers.
cards.example: Asking Facebook to find 1 million people who "look like" your current top 10% of buyers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A small piece of JavaScript placed on your site and run in the visitor's browser that records their visits so you can show them ads later on other platforms.
cards.example: Installing the Meta Pixel to track who visited your "Pricing" page but didn't buy.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The cost an advertiser pays for every 1,000 impressions of an advertisement.
cards.example: If a CPM is $10, you pay $10 for every 1,000 times your ad is shown.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A conversion that occurs after a user sees an ad but does not click it, then later converts on your site.
cards.example: A user seeing your YouTube ad, not clicking, but visiting your site via Google 2 days later to buy.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A conversion where a specific channel helped the user along the path, but was not the final click.
cards.example: Social media acting as an "assistant" by introducing the brand before the user bought via Google.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Parameters appended to the end of a URL (utm_source, utm_medium, utm_campaign, etc.) so that your analytics tool can identify the source, channel, and campaign the traffic came from.
cards.example: Adding "?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=launch" to your link to see in GA4 how many sales came from that post.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Google Tag Manager: A tag management system that allows you to quickly and easily update measurement codes and related code fragments.
cards.example: Using GTM to track button clicks without having to edit the website's HTML code.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Google Analytics 4: The current version of Google Analytics, which replaced Universal Analytics in 2023. Built on an event-based model, it measures websites and apps in a single property.
cards.example: Analyzing "Events" instead of "Sessions" to understand user behavior on a deep level.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: In GA4, the percentage of non-engaged sessions: under 10 seconds, no key event (conversion), and only one page viewed. It is exactly the inverse of the engagement rate.
cards.example: A user landing on a page, staying for 2 seconds, and leaving without clicking anything.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Data a customer deliberately and explicitly declares to a brand (preferences, interests, intentions), rather than being inferred from their behavior.
cards.example: A user answering a quiz on your site saying they prefer "Indoor Badminton" over "Outdoor".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Data a company collects itself by observing its customers on its own channels (website, app, CRM, store): browsing, purchases, subscriptions.
cards.example: Your list of email subscribers and their purchase history in your Shopify store.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Data collected, aggregated and resold by a third party (data broker, ad network) that has no direct relationship with the user.
cards.example: Buying a list of "High-income earners in France" from an external data provider (becoming harder with GDPR).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The principle that people trust what others have already chosen: showing ratings, reviews, client logos or user counts to reassure a hesitant visitor and get them to convert.
cards.example: Displaying a "Trustpilot 4.8/5" badge on your checkout page.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: FOMO: Fear Of Missing Out. The anxiety of missing an offer, an event or an experience that others are enjoying. Marketing triggers it with countdown timers, flash sales or social signals ("120 people are viewing this item").
cards.example: Adding a countdown timer that says "Sale ends in 2 hours!".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A psychological principle where the pain of losing is psychologically twice as powerful as the pleasure of gaining.
cards.example: Marketing a tool by saying "Stop losing $100 every day" instead of "Save $100 every day".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The mental discomfort experienced by a person who holds two or more contradictory beliefs; it often occurs after a purchase.
cards.example: A customer regretting an expensive purchase and looking for positive reviews to justify it.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A classic marketing model: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action.
cards.example: Structuring a LinkedIn post to grab attention with a hook, build interest with facts, and end with a CTA.
cards.cloze: A classic marketing model: {{c1::Attention, Interest, Desire, Action}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A three-step copywriting framework: Problem, Agitate, Solution. You name the reader's pain, make it feel unbearable, then present the offer as the way out.
cards.example: Identifying a pain point (Back pain), agitating it (It ruins your sleep), and offering the solution (Our chair).
cards.cloze: A three-step copywriting framework: {{c1::Problem, Agitate, Solution}}. You name the reader's pain, make it feel unbearable, then present the offer as the way out.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Jonah Berger's concept (Contagious): what sharing a piece of content or a brand earns a person in image and status. People share what makes them look interesting, smart or in the know, so brands create content worth showing off.
cards.example: Users sharing a "Year in Review" graphic from Spotify because it makes them look cool to their friends.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The number of new users an existing user generates. Formula: Number of Invites * Conversion Rate.
cards.example: If every 10 users bring in 12 new users, your virality coefficient is 1.2.
cards.cloze: The number of new users an existing user generates. Formula: {{c1::Number of Invites * Conversion Rate}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A business methodology in which user acquisition, expansion, conversion, and retention are driven primarily by the product itself.
cards.example: Zoom growing because people received invites to join meetings and then created their own accounts.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A business model where a basic service is provided free of charge, but money is charged for additional features.
cards.example: Spotify offering free music with ads, but charging for Spotify Premium.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A sales technique where a seller encourages the customer to purchase more expensive items or upgrades.
cards.example: Asking a customer "Would you like to upgrade to the Pro plan for only $5 more?".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A sales technique used to get a customer to spend more by purchasing a product that is related to what they are already buying.
cards.example: Suggesting a "Badminton Racket Bag" to someone who just bought a racket.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Net Promoter Score: A customer loyalty metric based on a single question, how likely you are to recommend the company, rated from 0 to 10. Formula: % Promoters - % Detractors.
cards.example: Asking customers "On a scale of 0-10, how likely are you to recommend us?".
cards.cloze: Net Promoter Score: A customer loyalty metric based on a single question, how likely you are to recommend the company, rated from 0 to 10. Formula: {{c1::% Promoters - % Detractors}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Classification of influencers by follower count. Common convention: Nano (1k-10k), Micro (10k-100k), Mid (100k-500k), Macro (500k-1M), Mega (1M+); thresholds vary from one agency to another.
cards.example: Choosing a Micro-influencer for higher engagement instead of a Mega-influencer for broad reach.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A metric that measures how many people interacted with a post relative to how many people actually saw it.
cards.example: A post seen by 100 people with 10 likes has a 10% engagement rate per reach.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A long-form, high-quality piece of content that covers a topic in depth and is broken down into smaller pieces.
cards.example: A 3,000-word guide on "Digital Marketing" that you turn into 10 LinkedIn posts and 1 video.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A group of interlinked web pages built around a central pillar page to improve SEO authority.
cards.example: Having a main "SEO Guide" page linking to sub-pages like "Technical SEO" and "On-Page SEO".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The number of pages on a website that Googlebot will crawl in a given timeframe.
cards.example: Ensuring your site loads fast so Google can crawl more of your important pages daily.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Canonical Tag: The HTML element link rel="canonical", placed in a page's head, that tells search engines the reference URL for that content to avoid duplicate content. It is the technical means; canonicalization is the process.
cards.example: Using rel="canonical" so Google knows which version of a product page to rank.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A permanent redirect (HTTP status 301) from one URL to another: it tells search engines the page has moved for good and passes most of its SEO value to the new address.
cards.example: Moving your blog from /old-blog to /new-blog and sending all traffic to the new address.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A text file created by webmasters to tell search engine bots how to crawl pages on their website.
cards.example: Using the file to tell Google NOT to crawl your "Admin" login page.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Structured data based on the schema.org vocabulary, added to a page's code (most often as JSON-LD), that helps search engines understand the content and show rich results.
cards.example: Adding a Recipe JSON-LD block to a recipe page so Google shows the star rating and cooking time in the SERP.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness: The criteria in Google's Search Quality Rater Guidelines for judging content quality. An evaluation framework, not a direct ranking score.
cards.example: Showing the credentials of the coach who wrote a fitness article to prove expertise.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Special results in Google that go beyond the standard blue link (Featured Snippets, Maps, Images, News).
cards.example: Winning a "Featured Snippet" that answers a user's question directly at the top of Google.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of optimizing your pages to appear in searches made through voice assistants like Siri or Alexa.
cards.example: Using natural, conversational phrases and long-tail keywords like "Where is the best badminton court?".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Google's practice of predominantly using the mobile version of a website's content for indexing and ranking.
cards.example: Ensuring your mobile site has the same content as your desktop site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A high-perceived-value lead magnet (tool, calculator, ready-to-use template) that attracts better-qualified leads, often in exchange for a business email through a form.
cards.example: Offering a "Revenue Calculator Spreadsheet" in exchange for a business email.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A low-priced offer (usually $1-$20) designed to turn a lead into a customer as quickly as possible.
cards.example: Selling a "90-minute marketing workshop" for $7 to build trust before selling a $500 course.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An enriched version of a persona that goes beyond demographics: daily routine, fears, goals, tools used and buying objections.
cards.example: "Persona: Freelance Sarah, uses Notion, fears missing tax deadlines, wants time-saving tools."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The constant personality a brand expresses across all its communications (e.g., expert, playful or blunt). It does not change from one channel or message to the next; only the tone adapts to context.
cards.example: Innocent Drinks talks like a funny friend on its bottles, its website and its social posts: the same playful personality is recognizable everywhere.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of a sale or a fixed fee paid to an affiliate for generating a transaction.
cards.example: Earning 15% for every referral who signs up for a digital marketing tool.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical analysis to estimate the impact of various marketing tactics on sales and then predict future results.
cards.example: Calculating how much TV ads, Facebook ads, and Radio ads each contributed to annual revenue.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A phenomenon where an audience sees the same ad too many times, leading to a drop in CTR and performance.
cards.example: After three weeks with the same visual, your Facebook ad's CTR drops from 2% to 0.6% and the CPC climbs: time to refresh the creative.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The average number of times a single person saw your ad over a given time period.
cards.example: If your frequency is 8, your audience is likely seeing your ad too often and getting annoyed.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The value Google Ads computes at each auction to decide whether your ad shows and in which position. Simplified formula: Bid Amount * Quality Score (Google also factors in thresholds, search context and the impact of assets).
cards.example: Winning the top spot on Google Search even with a lower bid because your ad is more relevant.
cards.cloze: The value Google Ads computes at each auction to decide whether your ad shows and in which position. Simplified formula: {{c1::Bid Amount * Quality Score}} (Google also factors in thresholds, search context and the impact of assets).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A 1 to 10 rating Google Ads gives each keyword to estimate how relevant your ads and landing page are. The higher it is, the less you pay for the same position.
cards.example: Improving your landing page speed to increase your Quality Score and lower your CPC.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Keywords that prevent your ad from being triggered by a certain word or phrase.
cards.example: Adding "Free" as a negative keyword so your paid ad doesn't show to people who don't want to buy.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The automated buying and selling of online ad space through software (DSPs, SSPs, ad exchanges) rather than human negotiation. Covers both real-time bidding (RTB) and guaranteed deals.
cards.example: Using a platform to automatically bid on banner space across thousands of websites in milliseconds.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Demand Side Platform: The advertiser-side software that automatically buys impressions (display, video, mobile, connected TV) across multiple ad exchanges, bidding according to your data and budget.
cards.example: Using The Trade Desk or Display & Video 360 to bid from a single interface on banners across thousands of websites.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Supply Side Platform: Software used by publishers to sell advertising space to advertisers in an automated way.
cards.example: A news website using an SSP to fill their sidebar with ads from the highest bidder.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Real-Time Bidding: The programmatic buying mode where each impression is auctioned individually, in milliseconds, at the moment the page loads.
cards.example: The millisecond-long auction that happens every time you load a webpage with an ad.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An auction where the highest bidder pays exactly what they bid.
cards.example: Bidding $2.00 and paying $2.00 even if the next highest bidder only bid $1.20.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An auction where the winner pays the price of the second-highest bid plus one cent.
cards.example: Bidding $2.00 and paying only $1.21 because the second bidder bid $1.20.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The portion of a market controlled by a particular company or product.
cards.example: If $1M is spent on Badminton rackets and your brand sells $200k, your market share is 20%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Statement of Work: A document that outlines the specific activities, deliverables, and timelines of a marketing project.
cards.example: A consultant sending an SOW to a client before starting a 3-month SEO audit.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Service Level Agreement: A contract between a service provider and a customer that defines the level of service expected.
cards.example: A marketing agency promising a 24-hour response time to all client emails.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Month-over-Month: A way to measure the growth of a metric compared to the previous month.
cards.example: Seeing a 10% MoM increase in website traffic from January to February.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Year-over-Year: A way to measure growth compared to the same period in the previous year.
cards.example: Comparing Black Friday sales in 2025 to Black Friday sales in 2024.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of comparing your business processes and performance metrics to industry bests or best practices from other companies.
cards.example: Comparing your email open rate of 20% to the industry average of 25%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An unconventional way of performing promotional activities on a very low budget.
cards.example: Using street graffiti or flash mobs to create buzz for a new rap album launch.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy in which an advertiser "ambushes" an event to compete for exposure against other advertisers.
cards.example: A brand giving out free shirts outside a stadium during the World Cup without being an official sponsor.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Direct to Consumer: When a brand sells directly to their end customers without going through retailers or wholesalers.
cards.example: Warby Parker or Dollar Shave Club selling via their own websites.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A multichannel approach to sales that seeks to provide customers with a seamless shopping experience across all channels.
cards.example: A customer being able to buy online and return the product in a physical store.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A product or service produced by one company that other companies rebrand to make it appear as if they had made it.
cards.example: A marketing agency selling an SEO tool under their own name that was actually built by another tech firm.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A landing page designed solely to capture email addresses from visitors.
cards.example: A page with nothing but a headline and a signup box for a newsletter.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: One specific form of social proof: named quotes from happy customers, with a first name, photo or job title, placed near a CTA to counter an objection and back up the promise.
cards.example: "This marketing course helped me land my first internship!" - Théo P.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A form of private equity and a type of financing that investors provide to startup companies and small businesses.
cards.example: A tech startup receiving $5M in funding to scale their AI marketing tool.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A founder's plan to sell their ownership in a company to investors or another company.
cards.example: A goal to have the startup acquired by Google within 5 years.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Starting a company with little capital and relying on personal savings and initial revenue to grow.
cards.example: Building your marketing agency without any outside investment or loans.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A specific problem that prospective customers of your business are experiencing.
cards.example: "I'm spending too much on ads and not getting any sales."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The primary goal a user has when typing a query into a search engine.
cards.example: Identifying if a user wants to "Buy" (Commercial intent) or just "Learn" (Informational intent).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advertisement or campaign that uses a subtle, low-pressure approach.
cards.example: A blog post that provides value and only mentions the product briefly at the end.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advertisement or campaign that uses a direct, high-pressure approach.
cards.example: A "Buy Now or Miss Out" email with aggressive language and bold colors.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Content whose main purpose is to attract attention and encourage visitors to click on a link to a particular web page.
cards.example: "You won't believe what happened next!" headlines that often disappoint the user.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Traffic that comes from private shares (messaging apps, email, SMS, closed groups) which analytics tools cannot attribute, and which therefore shows up as direct traffic.
cards.example: A link shared in a private WhatsApp group or Slack DM.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The act of blocking a user or their content from an online community in such a way that it is not readily apparent to the user that they have been banned.
cards.example: An Instagram account's posts suddenly not appearing in hashtags for no clear reason.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A search that ends without any click on a result: the user gets the answer directly on the SERP (snippet, AI Overview, weather, conversion, business listing).
cards.example: Searching "weather in Paris", reading the temperature right on Google and closing the tab without opening any site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Ratio comparing what a customer brings in over their lifetime with what it cost to acquire them. Formula: LTV / CAC. A ratio of about 3:1 is considered healthy.
cards.example: 1:1 means you are losing money after operational costs.
cards.cloze: Ratio comparing what a customer brings in over their lifetime with what it cost to acquire them. Formula: {{c1::LTV / CAC}}. A ratio of about 3:1 is considered healthy.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The time it takes for a customer to generate enough revenue to cover the cost of their acquisition.
cards.example: If CAC is $100 and a customer pays $10/month, the payback period is 10 months.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of users in a cohort who are still active after a certain period.
cards.example: Analyzing if the "Black Friday 2025" cohort has a higher 3-month retention than the "Summer Sale" cohort.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The amount of revenue lost from existing customers minus the revenue gained from expansions or upsells.
cards.example: A negative net churn means you are growing even without acquiring new customers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Additional revenue generated from existing customers through upsells or cross-sells.
cards.example: A customer upgrading from a "Starter" to a "Pro" plan.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Average Revenue Per User: A measure of the revenue generated per user or unit. Formula: Total Revenue / Total Users.
cards.example: A SaaS company tracking if their ARPU increases after launching a new premium feature.
cards.cloze: Average Revenue Per User: A measure of the revenue generated per user or unit. Formula: {{c1::Total Revenue / Total Users}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Average Revenue Per Paying User: Similar to ARPU but only counts users who have actually spent money.
cards.example: If you have 100 users but only 10 pay $10, your ARPU is $1 but your ARPPU is $10.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of newly acquired users who reached the "Activation" milestone.
cards.example: If 100 people download your app and 20 finish the onboarding, your activation rate is 20%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The single, lasting metric that best captures the core value your product delivers to customers, which the whole company aligns on for the long run.
cards.example: For Airbnb it's "Nights Booked"; for WhatsApp, "Messages Sent".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: One Metric That Matters: The single metric you focus all your attention on during a given phase, and which changes when the phase changes.
cards.example: Focusing 100% on "Email Signups" during a pre-launch phase.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: LVR: Lead Velocity Rate. The month-over-month growth percentage in the number of qualified leads generated. A leading indicator of future revenue, not a measure of funnel speed.
cards.example: Tracking if you are generating leads faster this month than last month to predict future revenue.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Marketing Qualified Lead: A lead who is more likely to become a customer compared to other leads based on marketing engagement.
cards.example: A lead who has downloaded 3 whitepapers and attended a webinar.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Sales Qualified Lead: A lead that the sales team has vetted and determined is ready for a direct sales follow-up.
cards.example: A lead who requested a pricing quote or a 1-on-1 demo.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Sales Accepted Lead: An MQL that the sales team agrees to take on because it meets the agreed criteria. The intermediate step between MQL and SQL.
cards.example: A lead that the sales team agrees to work on after a quick manual review.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A lead qualification framework: Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline.
cards.example: Asking a prospect if they have the budget and the power to sign a contract this quarter.
cards.cloze: A lead qualification framework: {{c1::Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A modern alternative to BANT: Challenges, Authority, Money, Prioritization.
cards.example: Focusing the sales conversation on the prospect's "Challenges" first.
cards.cloze: A modern alternative to BANT: {{c1::Challenges, Authority, Money, Prioritization}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The decrease in the value or validity of a lead over time.
cards.example: An old email list where 30% of the addresses no longer work.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A process where a user must confirm their email subscription by clicking a link in a confirmation email.
cards.example: Getting a higher-quality list and keeping proof of each subscriber's consent, useful under GDPR, even though the regulation does not require this mechanism.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A score mailbox providers (Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo…) assign to your sending domain and IP based on your spam complaints, bounces and recipient engagement. It determines whether you land in the inbox.
cards.example: If your reputation is low, your emails will go straight to the Spam folder.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance: a DNS record that builds on SPF and DKIM to tell receiving servers what to do with emails that fail (reject, quarantine) and sends you reports.
cards.example: Setting up DMARC to prevent hackers from spoofing your domain for phishing.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: DomainKeys Identified Mail: a cryptographic signature added to each email's header and checked against a public key published in DNS, proving the message really comes from your domain and was not altered.
cards.example: A digital "signature" that proves an email was actually sent by your brand.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Sender Policy Framework: A DNS record that lists the IP addresses allowed to send email on behalf of your domain.
cards.example: Adding Mailchimp's or Brevo's servers to your SPF record so they are allowed to send email on behalf of your domain.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Hard bounce: a permanent failure (invalid address), the address must be removed from the list. Soft bounce: a temporary failure (full inbox, server down), the send can be retried.
cards.example: Cleaning your list immediately after a hard bounce to protect your sender score.
cards.cloze: Hard bounce: a {{c1::permanent}} failure (invalid address), the address must be removed from the list. Soft bounce: a temporary failure (full inbox, server down), the send can be retried.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Dividing your email list based on actions taken, like "Opened last 3 emails" or "Clicked on Sale link".
cards.example: Sending a special discount only to "Engaged Non-Buyers".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The ability of an email to reach a recipient's primary inbox rather than being blocked or sent to spam.
cards.example: Setting up SPF, DKIM and DMARC (required by Gmail and Yahoo for bulk senders since 2024) and removing inactive addresses to improve your deliverability.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Ads that Google automatically generates based on the content of your website.
cards.example: Google seeing a new product on your site and creating an ad for it without you targeting keywords.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A goal-based campaign type that allows performance advertisers to access all of their Google Ads inventory from a single campaign.
cards.example: Letting AI decide whether to show your ad on YouTube, Search, or Gmail for the best ROI.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The widest keyword match type: your ad can show on any search related to the topic of your keyword, even with no words in common. Written without punctuation: tennis shoes.
cards.example: Targeting "badminton" might show your ad for "shuttlecock reviews" or "sports shoes".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The middle keyword match type: your ad shows on searches that include the meaning of your keyword, with other words before or after. Written in quotes: "tennis shoes".
cards.example: Targeting "tennis shoes" might show your ad for "buy tennis shoes" but not "running shoes".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The narrowest keyword match type: your ad only shows on searches with the same meaning or intent as your keyword. Written in brackets: [tennis shoes].
cards.example: Targeting [marketing coach] only shows your ad for "marketing coach" or very close variants.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The three components of the Google Ads Quality Score: Expected CTR, Ad Relevance, and Landing Page Experience. Each is rated below average, average, or above average.
cards.example: Improving your page load speed to boost the "Landing Page Experience" part of your score.
cards.cloze: The three components of the Google Ads Quality Score: {{c1::Expected CTR, Ad Relevance, and Landing Page Experience}}. Each is rated below average, average, or above average.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Additional information added to your Google Ads (sitelinks, phone number, location, prices). Google has called them "assets" instead of "extensions" since 2022.
cards.example: Adding "Sitelinks" to show your "Contact Us" and "Pricing" pages directly in the ad.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of impressions that your ads receive compared to the total number of impressions that your ads could get.
cards.example: If you have a 50% impression share, you are missing out on half the potential audience.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Target Cost Per Acquisition: A bidding strategy that sets bids to get as many conversions as possible at your set CPA.
cards.example: Telling Google "I want to pay $20 per lead, go find them for me".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Target Return on Ad Spend: A bidding strategy that sets bids to get as much revenue as possible at your set ROAS.
cards.example: Telling Google "I want a 400% return on my budget".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Conversions API: Meta's tool that sends events (purchase, lead, sign-up) directly from your server to Meta's servers, alongside the browser pixel, to keep tracking reliable despite ad blockers and iOS.
cards.example: Tracking sales even when a user has an AdBlocker or uses iOS 14+.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of sending tracking data from your server instead of the user's browser.
cards.example: Using a server GTM container to improve data accuracy and website speed.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Cookies created and stored by the website the user is visiting directly.
cards.example: Remembering a user's language preference on your own site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Cookies set by a domain other than the one the user is visiting, used for cross-site ad tracking. Blocked by default in Safari and Firefox; Chrome finally dropped its plan to remove them in 2025.
cards.example: Safari and Firefox blocking third-party cookies makes remarketing far less precise, hence the rise of server-side tracking.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The period of time after an ad interaction during which a conversion is recorded.
cards.example: A "7-day click" window means you get credit if the user buys within 7 days of clicking.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An attribution model that gives equal credit to every touchpoint in the customer journey.
cards.example: If a user saw 4 ads, each ad gets 25% of the credit for the sale.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An attribution model that gives more credit to touchpoints that happened closer in time to the conversion.
cards.example: The ad seen 1 hour before the purchase gets much more credit than the ad seen 2 weeks ago.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An attribution model that uses machine learning to evaluate all touchpoints and assign credit based on actual impact.
cards.example: Google’s default model that analyzes thousands of paths to see what truly drives sales.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Predictive Customer Lifetime Value: Using machine learning to forecast how much a customer will spend in the future.
cards.example: Identifying "Future VIPs" based on their first two purchases.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The measure of the lift that advertising spend provides, beyond what would have happened organically.
cards.example: Testing if you would have still made the sales if you turned off your Google Ads.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A survey-based method to measure the impact of an ad campaign on brand perception.
cards.example: Asking users "Have you heard of this brand?" after they saw a YouTube ad.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Formula (impressions-based variant): (Total Engagements / Total Impressions) * 100. Other calculations divide by follower count or by reach.
cards.example: A post with 50 likes/comments and 1,000 impressions has a 5% engagement rate.
cards.cloze: Formula (impressions-based variant): {{c1::(Total Engagements / Total Impressions) * 100}}. Other calculations divide by follower count or by reach.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: SOV: Share of Voice. The share your brand holds of a category's total visibility: mentions, impressions or ad spend, compared with all competitors combined. Not to be confused with market share, which measures sales.
cards.example: If there are 1,000 mentions of "Badminton" and 300 mention your brand, your SOV is 30%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When employees use their personal social media accounts to promote their company's news and products.
cards.example: Théo posting about his company's new AI features on his personal LinkedIn.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of building and maintaining an online community through interactions and content.
cards.example: Responding to every comment on a YouTube channel to build a loyal fanbase.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An editorial approach that favors timeless topics (guides, tutorials, definitions) over news, in order to build steady organic traffic that compounds year after year with minimal updating.
cards.example: Writing a "Complete Guide to SEO for Beginners" that will be useful for years.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An SEO strategy where you find high-ranking content, create something better, and then reach out to the right people to link to it.
cards.example: Seeing a "Top 10" list and creating a "Top 50" list that is more detailed.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Latent Semantic Indexing: SEO jargon for words and phrases semantically related to the primary keyword. The name is a misnomer, Google does not use LSI; the useful idea is covering the topic's semantic field.
cards.example: If you write about "Apple," LSI keywords like "iPhone," "Fruit," or "Steve Jobs" help Google understand the context.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency: A numerical statistic that reflects how important a word is to a document in a collection.
cards.example: A tool telling you to use the word "Algorithm" more often to rank for the keyword "AI Marketing".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A set of three metrics Google considers essential to a web page's user experience: LCP (loading), INP (responsiveness, which replaced FID in 2024) and CLS (visual stability).
cards.example: Fixing a layout shift so buttons don't move while the page is loading.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Largest Contentful Paint: Measures how long it takes for the largest element on the screen to load (Ideal: <2.5s).
cards.example: Optimizing the main hero image so it appears instantly for the user.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: First Input Delay: Former Core Web Vitals metric that measured the delay between a user's first interaction (click, key press) and the moment the browser starts responding. Replaced by INP (Interaction to Next Paint) in March 2024.
cards.example: Ensuring a user can click "Sign Up" immediately without the browser freezing.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Cumulative Layout Shift: Measures how much the visual layout of the page shifts during loading.
cards.example: Avoiding annoying "jumps" where text moves down because an ad finally loaded.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Linking from one page of your website to another page on the same website.
cards.example: Linking from your "Contact" page back to your "Home" page.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An outbound link: a link placed on one of your pages that points to a different website. The opposite of a backlink (a received link); citing reliable sources strengthens your content's credibility.
cards.example: Linking to a study on Forbes.com to back up your marketing claims.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A link carrying the rel="nofollow" attribute, asking search engines not to pass authority (link juice) to the linked page. Since 2019 Google treats it as a hint rather than a strict directive.
cards.example: Adding rel="nofollow" to links in your blog comments (and rel="sponsored" to paid links) so you don't vouch for those links to Google.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The default state of a link ("dofollow" is not a real HTML attribute): without rel="nofollow", search engines can follow it and pass authority to the destination page.
cards.example: A plain link with no rel="nofollow", rel="sponsored" or rel="ugc": Google can follow it and give it weight.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A metric from Ahrefs that shows the strength of a website's backlink profile on a scale of 0 to 100.
cards.example: A website with a DR of 80 is very difficult to outrank.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of searchers who click on an organic search result.
cards.example: Improving your Title Tag to get more clicks than the result above you.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The frequency and magnitude of changes in search engine results pages.
cards.example: A major Google Algorithm Update causing rankings to jump up and down for a week.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A group of websites that all link to each other or to a specific page to fake popularity.
cards.example: A network of 200 empty sites created only to link to each other and to your store: a tactic that can earn a manual penalty from Google.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of using "Black Hat" techniques on a competitor's website to get them penalized by Google.
cards.example: A competitor buying thousands of spammy links for your site to hurt your rankings.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A Google tool that allows you to tell search engines to ignore certain toxic backlinks.
cards.example: Using the disavow tool to clean up a site after a negative SEO attack.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of checking a website's technical health to ensure search engines can crawl and index it.
cards.example: Checking for 404 errors, slow pages, and duplicate content.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An HTML attribute used to specify the language and geographical targeting of a webpage.
cards.example: Telling Google that one page is for French speakers and another is for English speakers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Content that has little or no value to the user, often created just to target keywords.
cards.example: A 100-word page that provides no real information.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When a user clicks on a search result and then immediately clicks "back" to the SERP because the page wasn't helpful.
cards.example: You search "pancake recipe", open the first result, find no recipe, hit back and click the second result instead.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The amount of time a user spends on a page after clicking a link in the SERP before returning to the results.
cards.example: A three-minute dwell time on your article: the user read it before returning to the results. Google says it does not use it directly as a ranking factor.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of identifying keywords that your competitors rank for, but you do not.
cards.example: Finding out your competitor is getting 1,000 visits/month for a term you haven't written about.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: In-depth content that is usually over 1,500 or 2,000 words.
cards.example: Writing a massive "Ultimate Guide" to attract more backlinks and authority.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The decline in organic traffic to a piece of content over time as it becomes outdated.
cards.example: Your 2022 "Best AI tools" article dropped from 5,000 to 800 organic visits a month by 2026: that is content decay, and you refresh it to climb back.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Valuable content that is hidden behind a form and requires user information to access.
cards.example: A "Premium Report" that requires an email and phone number to download.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of people who downloaded or requested the lead magnet among those who saw it (popup, page or banner). Formula: (downloads / views) * 100.
cards.example: If 100 people saw the popup and 10 signed up, the lead magnet conversion rate is 10%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The likelihood of previous customers to continue to buy from a specific brand.
cards.example: A customer who refuses to buy any other coffee brand besides Starbucks.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When customers are so happy with a brand that they actively promote it to others without being paid.
cards.example: A fan of a specific badminton racket who spontaneously posts a glowing review on a forum and recommends it to their club, without getting anything in return.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The use of natural language processing to automatically classify texts (reviews, comments, mentions) by the opinion they express: positive, negative or neutral.
cards.example: Analyzing mentions on X (formerly Twitter) to see if people are happy or angry about a new product launch.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Customers who give a score of 9 or 10 on the NPS survey.
cards.example: Your most loyal fans who will recommend you to everyone.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Customers who give a score of 7 or 8 on the NPS survey.
cards.example: Customers who are satisfied but could easily switch to a competitor.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Customers who give a score of 0 to 6 on the NPS survey.
cards.example: Unhappy customers who might damage your brand with bad reviews.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Customer Satisfaction Score: A metric measuring satisfaction with a specific product or interaction through a rating (often 1 to 5). The score is the percentage of satisfied answers.
cards.example: Asking "How satisfied were you with your support call today?".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Customer Effort Score: A metric that measures how much effort a customer had to put in to resolve an issue or complete a task.
cards.example: Asking "How easy was it to get your refund?".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Share of customers lost over a period, compared with the customers you had at the start. Formula: (Lost Customers / Total Customers at Start of Period) * 100.
cards.example: Losing 10 out of 100 customers in a month equals a 10% churn rate.
cards.cloze: Share of customers lost over a period, compared with the customers you had at the start. Formula: {{c1::(Lost Customers / Total Customers at Start of Period) * 100}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The amount of recurring revenue lost when customers cancel or downgrade, without subtracting expansion (gross churn). Measured in money, not in number of customers.
cards.example: Tracking if you are losing your "Big Spenders" or just "Small Spenders".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The number of customer accounts (companies or individuals) lost over a period, regardless of how much revenue each one brought. Counts customers, where revenue churn counts money.
cards.example: Losing 5 small clients while keeping your 1 big client.

cards.subject: ia
