cards.definition: A branch of statistics for analyzing the expected duration of time until an event (like a churn) occurs.
cards.example: Predicting that most users will churn after the 4th month of a subscription.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Unsupervised clustering algorithm that splits data into K groups, chosen in advance, by assigning each point to the nearest center (centroid). Used to segment customers by similarity.
cards.example: With K = 3, automatically finding three groups of users: "Gamers", "Professionals" and "Students".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A statistical process for estimating the relationships among variables.
cards.example: Predicting how much sales will increase if you increase your ad spend by $1,000.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A measure of how spread out your data is (e.g., are all your sales $50, or are they $5 and $500?).
cards.example: Understanding if your "Average Order Value" is misleading because of a few huge orders.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The property of a test result too unlikely under the null hypothesis to be put down to chance: its p-value falls below the chosen threshold (often 0.05). A significant result is not necessarily a large one.
cards.example: In an A/B test, ensuring the "Winning" version really is better and wasn't just lucky.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The certainty threshold set before a test, usually 95%: it is 1 minus the accepted risk of declaring a variant the winner when it is not (5%). The higher it is, the more traffic you need.
cards.example: Your A/B testing tool shows 'B wins, 95% confidence': there would be less than a 5% chance of seeing such a gap if A and B were actually equivalent.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The probability of obtaining test results at least as extreme as the results actually observed, under the assumption that the null hypothesis is correct.
cards.example: In A/B testing, a p-value below 0.05 usually means your test is statistically significant.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The number of observations or individuals included in a study or experiment.
cards.example: Realizing your A/B test is invalid because only 10 people saw it.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A test that changes several page elements at once (headline, image, button…) and compares all their combinations to measure each one's effect and their interactions. It needs far more traffic than an A/B test.
cards.example: Testing 3 headlines AND 2 button colors at the same time (requires a lot of traffic).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An inspection method in which one or more experts check an interface against a list of recognised usability principles (Nielsen's 10 heuristics, for instance), without testing on real users.
cards.example: A UX expert reviewing a landing page against Nielsen's heuristics and flagging 5 obvious "friction points", such as an error message that doesn't say what to fix.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Any element of a website that confuses, distracts, or prevents a user from converting.
cards.example: A 15-field checkout form is a major source of friction.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The amount of mental effort being used in the working memory.
cards.example: A website with 10 different flashing banners creates too much cognitive load for the user.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique that records, with a specialised camera, where a user's gaze lands on a screen and in what order, to learn what they see, read or ignore on a page.
cards.example: Seeing that users never look at the right sidebar of your blog.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The tendency of users to read web content in an "F" shape (scanning the top and then down the left side).
cards.example: Placing your most important message in the first two paragraphs.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A pattern where the eye travels from top-left to top-right, then down-left, then bottom-right.
cards.example: Commonly used for simple landing pages with a clear CTA at the end.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The design of products and environments for people with disabilities.
cards.example: Ensuring your website can be navigated by someone using a screen reader.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An approach to web design that makes web pages render well on a variety of devices and window or screen sizes.
cards.example: A site that looks perfect on an iPhone, an iPad, and a 27-inch monitor.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Accelerated Mobile Pages: an open-source HTML framework launched by Google in 2015 to build stripped-down pages that load almost instantly on mobile. Now in decline, superseded by Core Web Vitals.
cards.example: Google used to require AMP for the Top Stories carousel and showed a lightning-bolt icon; that ended in 2021 and many publishers have dropped it.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A website that, thanks to a service worker and a manifest, can be installed on the home screen, work offline and send push notifications like a native app, without going through an app store.
cards.example: A website that acts like a mobile app and can work offline.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Application Programming Interface: A set of functions that allows applications to access data and interact with external software components.
cards.example: Connecting your CRM to your Email tool so they can "talk" to each other.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An HTTP notification an application automatically sends to a URL you choose as soon as an event happens (order, form submission), so you don't have to keep polling its API.
cards.example: Sending a notification to Slack the exact second a new sale happens in Shopify.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: JavaScript Object Notation: A lightweight data-interchange format.
cards.example: The format used to send data from a website to a tracking server.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: HyperText Markup Language: The standard markup language for documents designed to be displayed in a web browser.
cards.example: Editing the href attribute of a link tag (a) to change where the link points.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Cascading Style Sheets: A style sheet language used for describing the presentation of a document written in HTML.
cards.example: Changing the “.button” class to make all your buttons blue.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A programming language that allows you to implement complex features on web pages (interactivity).
cards.example: Using JS to trigger a popup when a user tries to leave your page.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Document Object Model: the tree representation of an HTML page loaded in the browser, which JavaScript (or a tool like GTM) can read and modify element by element.
cards.example: GTM uses the DOM to find specific elements on a page to track.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A back-end only content management system that acts as a content repository, making content accessible via an API.
cards.example: Storing your blog posts in one place and displaying them on both your website and your mobile app.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A website that interacts with the user by dynamically rewriting the current page rather than loading entire new pages from a server.
cards.example: Gmail or Facebook, where the page doesn't "refresh" when you click a folder.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A series of redirects between the initial URL and the destination URL.
cards.example: URL A -> URL B -> URL C (this slows down the site and hurts SEO).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process by which a site (or Google itself) chooses the reference URL among several versions of the same content: http or https, with or without www, with or without parameters. The canonical tag, 301 redirects and internal links all feed into it.
cards.example: Ensuring all versions of your site point to the official “https://www.site.com”.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Whether a page, once crawled, can be added to the search engine's index. A noindex tag, a canonical pointing to another URL or an HTTP error block it.
cards.example: A page with a "noindex" tag has zero indexability.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Whether a search engine bot can reach a page and read its content: the step before indexing. A robots.txt block or a lack of links to the page prevents it.
cards.example: A site with a broken navigation menu might have poor crawlability.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: XML Sitemap: The XML-format file (often sitemap.xml) listing a site's important URLs with their last update date, submitted to Google Search Console to make crawling easier.
cards.example: Submitting https://site.com/sitemap.xml in Google Search Console and regenerating it every time you publish a new post.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A business model where brands sell directly to customers, bypassing traditional "middlemen" like retailers.
cards.example: A brand like Tesla that sells cars directly to people without dealerships.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Business-to-Business-to-Consumer: A model where a business sells to another business, but with the goal of reaching the end consumer.
cards.example: Intel selling chips to Dell, so Dell can sell computers to people.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Using AI and real-time data to provide extremely relevant content or product suggestions to an individual.
cards.example: Netflix showing you a different thumbnail for a movie based on your favorite genre.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of varying the price for a product or service to reflect changing market conditions.
cards.example: Airlines raising ticket prices as the plane fills up or as the date gets closer.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A measure of how much the quantity demanded of a good responds to a change in the price of that good.
cards.example: If you raise prices by 10% and lose 50% of your customers, your price elasticity is high.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A visual representation of every touchpoint a customer has with your brand.
cards.example: Mapping the path from "Saw a LinkedIn post" to "Signed a $10k contract".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Any point of interaction between a buyer and a seller.
cards.example: A physical store, a Facebook ad, a support chat, or an unboxing experience.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The systematic distortion introduced by the chosen attribution model: for example, last click over-credits branded search and undervalues discovery channels (video, social).
cards.example: Cutting your YouTube ads because the "last click" report credits them with 0 sales, even though they are what makes people discover the brand.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The bias introduced by the selection of individuals, groups, or data for analysis.
cards.example: Doing a survey of your "Best Customers" and thinking everyone loves your product.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The tendency to search for, interpret, favor, and recall information in a way that confirms one's preexisting beliefs.
cards.example: A marketer only looking at "Likes" to prove a campaign was a success, while ignoring "Sales".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The logical error of concentrating on the people or things that "survived" some process and inadvertently overlooking those that did not.
cards.example: Studying only successful startups and ignoring the 90% that failed.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Cognitive bias where one perceived positive trait (fame, a nice design, one successful product) colours the judgement of every other quality of a person or brand, without evidence.
cards.example: Thinking a product is high quality just because the company's CEO is famous.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A cognitive bias where an individual relies too heavily on an initial piece of information (the "anchor") when making decisions.
cards.example: Showing a "crossed out" price of $100 so the $20 price looks like a huge bargain.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A social norm of responding to a positive action with another positive action.
cards.example: Giving away a free high-quality e-book so the user feels "obligated" to buy your course.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Persuasion principle (Cialdini) whereby something looks more desirable when its quantity or access is limited: remaining stock, limited edition, invite-only access. Perceived value rises with scarcity.
cards.example: "Only 3 items left in stock!".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The tendency to obey and trust people who are perceived as experts.
cards.example: Using a doctor or a professional athlete to endorse a health product.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The desire to be (and to appear) consistent with what we have already done.
cards.example: Asking a user for a small "Yes" (a free trial) to make them more likely to say a big "Yes" later.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The principle that we are more likely to be persuaded by people we like.
cards.example: Using "About Us" pages to show the human side of a marketing agency.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The portion of an individual's self-concept derived from perceived membership in a relevant social group.
cards.example: Creating a "Tribe" of badminton players who all use the same brand.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A good for which demand increases as the price increases, because of its exclusive nature and appeal as a status symbol.
cards.example: Luxury watches or designer handbags.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The degree to which your brand is thought about or noticed when a customer is in a buying situation.
cards.example: Being the first brand someone thinks of when they need "Badminton shoes".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The weakening of a brand through its overuse or through being associated with poor-quality products.
cards.example: A luxury brand starting to sell cheap products in supermarkets.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A marketing partnership between at least two different brands of goods or services.
cards.example: The "Nike + Apple Watch" partnership.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When a company buys a product from another company and rebrands it as their own.
cards.example: An agency using a generic "SEO Audit" tool but putting their own logo on the reports.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A measure of how much a product or service is being used by customers compared to the total estimated market.
cards.example: Calculating that only 1% of UK badminton players have bought your racket.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The simultaneous pursuit of differentiation and low cost to open up a new market space and create new demand.
cards.example: Creating a market where there is no competition (e.g., Cirque du Soleil).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Competing in existing industries with intense competition and "bloody" price wars.
cards.example: Trying to launch a new generic Cola brand against Coca-Cola and Pepsi.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The advantage gained by the first significant occupant of a market segment.
cards.example: Amazon being the first major online bookstore.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The phenomenon where a product or service becomes more valuable to its users as more people use it.
cards.example: Facebook, LinkedIn, or eBay are only useful because other people are on them.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The cost advantages that enterprises obtain due to their scale of operation, with cost per unit of output decreasing as scale increases.
cards.example: A large company being able to buy ads 50% cheaper than a small startup.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Total Addressable Market: The total revenue opportunity that is available to a product or service.
cards.example: The total amount spent on "Badminton gear" worldwide annually.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Serviceable Addressable Market: The portion of TAM your offer can actually serve, given your geographic reach, your channels and regulatory constraints.
cards.example: The total amount spent on "Badminton gear" in France specifically.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Serviceable Obtainable Market: The portion of SAM that you can actually capture.
cards.example: The realistic percentage of French badminton players you can reach with your current budget.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Number of months of gross margin needed to earn back the cost of acquiring a customer. Formula: CAC / (ARPU * Gross Margin).
cards.example: CAC of $120, ARPU of $20/month, 75% gross margin: 120 / (20 × 0.75) = 8 months to pay back the customer.
cards.cloze: Number of months of gross margin needed to earn back the cost of acquiring a customer. Formula: {{c1::CAC / (ARPU * Gross Margin)}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The rate at which a company is losing money in a negative cash flow situation.
cards.example: A startup spending $50k/month more than it earns while trying to grow.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The amount of time a company has before it runs out of money, based on its burn rate.
cards.example: "We have $500k in the bank and spend $50k/month, so we have 10 months of runway."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A fundamental change in a business's strategy when its current products or services are not meeting the market's needs.
cards.example: A company shifting from a "Badminton App" to a "General Sports Tracking App".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A privately held startup company with a current valuation of US$1 billion or more.
cards.example: Companies like Uber, Airbnb, or Canva before they went public.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Minimum Viable Product: A version of a product with just enough features to be usable by early customers who can then provide feedback.
cards.example: Launching a simple 1-page website to see if people want to buy your coaching.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The degree to which a product satisfies a strong market demand.
cards.example: The moment when you stop "pushing" your product and customers start "pulling" it from you.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Go-To-Market Strategy: A plan that details how a company will launch a new product to a specific audience.
cards.example: Defining that you will use LinkedIn ads and cold email to launch your new SaaS tool.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A loss in sales caused by a company's introduction of a new product that displaces one of its own older products.
cards.example: Apple's iPhone sales hurting their own iPod sales.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When a company expands its business into different steps on the same production path.
cards.example: A badminton brand buying the factory that makes their shuttlecocks.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of a company increasing production of goods or services at the same part of the supply chain via internal expansion, merger or acquisition.
cards.example: A marketing agency buying another marketing agency to get more clients.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A framework used to evaluate a company's competitive position: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats.
cards.example: Realizing your "Strength" is AI expertise but your "Threat" is a new privacy law.
cards.cloze: A framework used to evaluate a company's competitive position: {{c1::Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A framework to analyze the external environment: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal.
cards.example: Analyzing how "Legal" changes in GDPR affect your data strategy.
cards.cloze: A framework to analyze the external environment: {{c1::Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A pricing strategy in which a marketer sets a relatively high initial price for a product or service at first, then lowers the price over time.
cards.example: Apple releasing the newest iPhone at $1,200 and lowering the price when the next model comes out.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Setting a low initial price for a new product to attract customers and gain market share quickly.
cards.example: A new streaming service launching at $1/month to steal users from Netflix.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of free users who eventually upgrade to a paid plan.
cards.example: If 1% of Spotify Free users upgrade to Premium, the freemium conversion rate is 1%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The stage of the funnel where you focus on increasing the value of each customer.
cards.example: Implementing annual billing to get more cash upfront from your subscribers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Ensuring the user has a "Great First Experience".
cards.example: Sending a personalized "Welcome Video" immediately after a user signs up.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The cycle of collecting customer feedback (suggestions, complaints), turning it into product improvements, then telling customers what changed so the cycle starts again.
cards.example: Reading app store reviews and fixing the bugs that users mention.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Grouping users by what they DO rather than when they joined.
cards.example: Comparing users who "Completed 1 workout" vs those who "Completed 10 workouts".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of investigating why customers are leaving your business.
cards.example: Interviewing customers who canceled to find out if they left because of price or features.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A marketing campaign specifically designed to keep customers who are at risk of leaving, or to win back those who have just canceled.
cards.example: Sending a "We miss you" email with a 50% discount to users who haven't logged in for 30 days.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A marketing technique used to determine which customers are the best ones by examining Recency, Frequency, and Monetary Value.
cards.example: Identifying your "Champions" (bought recently, buy often, spend a lot).
cards.cloze: A marketing technique used to determine which customers are the best ones by examining {{c1::Recency, Frequency, and Monetary Value}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The ideal target ratio for a scaling SaaS company is generally 3:1.
cards.example: Realizing your 10:1 ratio means you are under-investing in marketing and could grow faster.
cards.cloze: The ideal target ratio for a scaling SaaS company is generally {{c1::3:1}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: How quickly leads move from one stage of the sales funnel to the next, up to purchase. Measures elapsed time, unlike LVR, which measures growth in the number of leads.
cards.example: Measuring how many days it takes for a "New Lead" to become a "Paying Customer".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The amount of time it takes from the first contact with a prospect to closing the deal.
cards.example: A B2B sales cycle of 6 months for an enterprise software contract.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A visual representation of where your prospects are in the sales process.
cards.example: Tracking $1M worth of "Potential Deals" in your CRM.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of opportunities (deals) in your pipeline that end in a won sale rather than a lost one. Calculated on deals, not on raw leads.
cards.example: If you have 100 deals in your pipeline and close 20, your win rate is 20%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The average amount of revenue generated by a single closed sale.
cards.example: Aiming to increase your "Average Deal Size" from $5k to $10k by targeting larger companies.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of providing the sales team with the information, content, and tools that help them sell more effectively.
cards.example: Creating a "Sales Deck" or "Case Study" for the sales team to show to prospects.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A type of marketing designed to elicit an instant response by encouraging prospects to take a specific action.
cards.example: A Facebook ad with a "Shop Now" button that leads to a purchase.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Branding is about long-term awareness; Direct Response is about immediate action.
cards.example: Using a TV ad for branding and a Google ad for direct response.
cards.cloze: {{c1::Branding}} is about long-term awareness; Direct Response is about immediate action.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advertising approach where the ad is chosen based on the topic of the page it appears on, not on the visitor's profile or browsing history. Works without cookies or personal data.
cards.example: Showing an ad for "Badminton rackets" on a news article about the Olympic Badminton finals.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A direct deal between an advertiser and a publisher where the advertiser agrees to buy a specific number of impressions.
cards.example: Buying 1 million impressions on a specific tech news site for a fixed price.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An invite-only auction where high-quality publishers make their ad inventory available to a select group of advertisers.
cards.example: Being invited to bid on ad space on the New York Times website.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique that allows publishers to offer their ad space to multiple ad exchanges simultaneously before making a call to their ad server.
cards.example: With Prebid.js, a news site has eight ad exchanges compete on every impression before Google Ad Manager assigns the slot.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An open digital marketplace where advertisers' DSPs and publishers' SSPs trade impressions through real-time auctions (e.g., Google AdX, OpenX, Xandr).
cards.example: The "Stock Exchange" of digital ads (e.g., Google AdX, OpenX).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The total amount of ad space a publisher has available to sell to advertisers.
cards.example: A website having 3 banner spots on every page that they need to fill.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The portion of a web page that is visible without scrolling down.
cards.example: Placing your most important CTA "Above the Fold" to ensure everyone sees it.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The portion of a web page that requires scrolling to be seen.
cards.example: Placing detailed reviews and technical specs "Below the Fold".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A full-screen ad that covers the interface of their host app or site.
cards.example: The annoying ads that pop up and cover the whole screen while you are playing a mobile game.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The concrete placement format a platform offers to insert an ad into its content stream: a sponsored post in a feed, a Promoted Tweet, a sponsored search result, a "recommended for you" widget.
cards.example: An ad that looks just like a regular post in your Instagram feed.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An ad that plays before the main video content that a user has selected.
cards.example: A 15-second unskippable ad before a YouTube video starts.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An ad that plays during the middle of a video.
cards.example: An ad break in the middle of a 30-minute podcast or YouTube video.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An ad that plays after the video content has finished.
cards.example: A short ad that appears at the very end of a tutorial video.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A short, unskippable 6-second video ad on YouTube.
cards.example: Using a quick "6-second" clip to increase brand awareness at a low cost.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A feature that limits the number of times a specific user sees an ad within a given time period.
cards.example: Telling Facebook "Don't show this ad to the same person more than twice a day".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of scheduling ads for specific times of the day or days of the week.
cards.example: Only showing your "Lunch Special" ads between 11:00 AM and 2:00 PM.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique that draws a virtual boundary (GPS, Wi-Fi, RFID) around a specific location and triggers an action, an ad or a notification, when a mobile device enters or leaves the zone.
cards.example: Sending a mobile notification to people when they walk within 100 meters of your store.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Targeting an audience in a very small, specific geographic area (like a single neighborhood or street).
cards.example: For your gym opening, targeting on Meta only the residents of the Croix-Rousse neighborhood in Lyon.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A targeting setting (on the Google Display Network, for instance) where you supply a list of keywords and your ads only show on pages whose text contains those words.
cards.example: Showing ads for "Badminton coaching" only on websites that mention the word "Badminton".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Targeting users based on their long-term interests and hobbies.
cards.example: Targeting people who have shown a consistent interest in "American Rap" and "Sneakers".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Targeting users based on their past actions, such as websites visited or products purchased.
cards.example: Targeting people who have "Recently traveled to Spain" or "Downloaded a marketing app".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An audience built using your own data (email list, website visitors, app users).
cards.example: Uploading your list of 5,000 customers to Facebook to show them a "New Arrival" ad.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy where you show a series of different ads to a user over time.
cards.example: Day 1: Show a Brand Video. Day 3: Show a Testimonial. Day 7: Show a Discount.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Showing ads to users that contain the exact products they viewed on your website.
cards.example: Showing a user the specific pair of red sneakers they just looked at on your e-commerce site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The set of methods (deterministic or probabilistic) that link one person's visits across several devices, in order to rebuild a single journey from the ad to the purchase.
cards.example: Knowing that a user clicked an ad on their phone but finally bought on their laptop.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Linking two devices to the same person by statistical inference, from technical signals (IP address, browser, location, timing), with no certain identifier. Less accurate than deterministic tracking.
cards.example: Assuming that an iPhone and a MacBook on the same home Wi-Fi, with the same language and city, belong to the same person.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Identifying a user across devices because they have logged into the same account (e.g., Facebook or Google).
cards.example: A user logged into their account on their phone and then on their PC: both visits are linked with certainty thanks to the login ID.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Tracking user behavior without the use of cookies, often using server-side data or digital fingerprinting.
cards.example: Using a unique ID generated from a user's browser settings to track them.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique used to identify a user based on unique characteristics of their browser and device (fonts, screen resolution).
cards.example: A controversial tracking method that is being blocked by many modern browsers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The specific platform where the traffic originated (e.g., "google", "linkedin", "newsletter").
cards.example: Using “utm_source=linkedin” to see how many clicks your post generated.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The type of marketing channel (e.g., "cpc", "social", "email", "organic").
cards.example: Using “utm_medium=email” to distinguish your newsletter from your social posts.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The specific name of the marketing effort (e.g., "summer_sale_2026").
cards.example: Using “utm_campaign=black_friday” to track all traffic related to that specific event.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of measuring specific interactions on a website, such as button clicks, video plays, or form submissions.
cards.example: Setting up a GA4 "Event" to track how many people click the "Play" button on your podcast.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A feature in GA4 that automatically tracks common events like scrolls, outbound clicks, and site searches.
cards.example: Enabling "Scroll Tracking" without having to write any code in GTM.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A descriptive attribute of data that you can define in GA4 to track things Google doesn't track by default.
cards.example: Creating a dimension for "Author Name" so you can see which of your bloggers gets the most traffic.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A numerical value that you define in GA4 to track specific business goals.
cards.example: Creating a metric for "Points Earned" in a loyalty program.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The flow of data from your website or app to your GA4 property.
cards.example: Setting up one data stream for your website and another for your iOS app.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: In GA4, the percentage of "engaged sessions": over 10 seconds, or a key event (conversion), or at least 2 page views. It is the complement of the GA4 bounce rate.
cards.example: A 45-second session on an article counts as engaged, even if the visitor only views one page.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A collection of advanced techniques that go beyond standard reports to help you uncover deeper insights about customer behavior.
cards.example: Using a "Path Exploration" to see exactly which pages users visit before they buy.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Google's serverless, highly scalable data warehouse that allows for super-fast SQL queries of large datasets.
cards.example: Exporting your GA4 data to BigQuery to perform advanced data science analysis.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A query language used to retrieve, filter and manipulate the data stored in a relational database.
cards.example: Writing a query to find "All customers who spent more than $500 last month".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The graphical representation of information and data (charts, graphs, maps).
cards.example: Showing your traffic trend over 12 months as a line chart rather than a table of 12 numbers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A free tool from Google that turns your data into informative, easy to read, easy to share, and fully customizable dashboards.
cards.example: Connecting your Google Ads and GA4 to one beautiful report for your boss.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A visual display of the most important information needed to achieve one or more objectives.
cards.example: A "Daily KPI Dashboard" that shows Revenue, CAC, and ROAS in real-time.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique used to identify unusual patterns that do not conform to expected behavior.
cards.example: An automated alert telling you that your website traffic suddenly dropped by 90% (might be a bug).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The use of data, statistical algorithms, and machine learning techniques to identify the likelihood of future outcomes.
cards.example: Predicting which customers will buy again next month based on their past history.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A type of AI that allows software applications to become more accurate at predicting outcomes without being explicitly programmed.
cards.example: Google Ads using ML to decide exactly which person should see your ad.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The simulation of human intelligence processes by machines, especially computer systems.
cards.example: Gmail's spam filter, your phone's voice recognition or ChatGPT are all applications of AI.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Large Language Model: a transformer-based neural network trained on huge text corpora to predict and generate text, the engine behind assistants like ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude.
cards.example: GPT-5, Gemini and Claude are LLMs.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of refining and optimizing the input given to an AI to get the best possible output.
cards.example: Writing a 5-step instruction for an AI to act as a Marketing Consultant.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Natural Language Processing: the branch of AI that lets machines analyze and produce human language: sentiment analysis, translation, entity extraction. LLMs are its most recent tool.
cards.example: Using NLP to automatically categorize 1,000 customer reviews into "Positive" or "Negative".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: AI that can create new content, such as text, images, video, or audio.
cards.example: Using Midjourney to create a unique hero image for your landing page.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Asking an AI to perform a task without giving it any examples.
cards.example: "Write a poem about badminton."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Providing an AI with a few examples of the task you want it to perform before asking for the final output.
cards.example: Giving an AI 3 examples of a good meta description before asking it to write 10 more.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A prompting technique where you ask the AI to "think step-by-step" to solve a complex problem.
cards.example: Asking an AI: "Before suggesting a budget, reason step by step: first compute the cost per lead, compare it with the average order value, then conclude."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When an AI generates incorrect or nonsensical information but presents it as a fact.
cards.example: An AI making up a fake marketing term that doesn't actually exist.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of ensuring that AI is developed and used in a way that is fair, transparent, and accountable.
cards.example: Avoiding bias in your marketing algorithms so you don't unfairly target specific groups.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An image, video or voice generated or altered by AI to make a real person appear to say or do something they never said or did.
cards.example: A fake video of a celebrity endorsing a crypto scam, run as an ad without their consent.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An umbrella term for the automated production of ad creatives: generating variants, adapting them to formats and testing them at scale, often before the campaign runs.
cards.example: Testing 1,000 different ad variations automatically to see which one works best.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technology that assembles the ad at impression time, picking its elements (image, headline, offer) from the viewer's data: location, weather, time of day, product viewed.
cards.example: Changing the background color of an ad based on the weather in the user's city.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A computer program designed to simulate conversation with human users, especially over the Internet.
cards.example: Using an AI chatbot to handle 80% of your customer support questions.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method of engaging with website visitors and converting leads via dialogue-driven activities (like live chat).
cards.example: Using a "Welcome Chat" to ask users what they are looking for and guide them to the right product.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy that connects every channel (website, app, email, social media, physical store) into one seamless, consistent experience, each channel aware of what happened on the others. Unlike multichannel, where channels run in silos.
cards.example: Ensuring your brand looks and feels the same on Instagram, Email, and in your physical shop.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The totality of a customer's individual perceptions of their relationship with a brand.
cards.example: Ensuring that every step from "Seeing an ad" to "Getting a refund" is smooth and pleasant.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A research approach that collects and analyzes what customers express (needs, expectations, pain points) through interviews, surveys or reviews, before decisions are made.
cards.example: Conducting 1-on-1 interviews with your top 10% of customers to understand why they stay.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of recurring revenue retained from existing customers over a given period. Formula: (Starting MRR + Expansion - Contraction - Churn) / Starting MRR.
cards.example: An NRR over 100% means your business is growing even without new customers.
cards.cloze: The percentage of recurring revenue retained from existing customers over a given period. Formula: {{c1::(Starting MRR + Expansion - Contraction - Churn) / Starting MRR}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of recurring revenue retained from existing customers, excluding expansion. Formula: (Starting MRR - Churn - Contraction) / Starting MRR.
cards.example: GRR can never be higher than 100%.
cards.cloze: The percentage of recurring revenue retained from existing customers, excluding expansion. Formula: {{c1::(Starting MRR - Churn - Contraction) / Starting MRR}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Monthly Recurring Revenue: The predictable total revenue generated by your business from all the active subscriptions in a particular month.
cards.example: A SaaS company with 1,000 users paying $10/month has an MRR of $10k.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Annual Recurring Revenue: The yearly version of MRR.
cards.example: A company with $100k MRR has an ARR of $1.2M.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Quick estimate of the revenue a customer brings in over their whole relationship with you. Formula: ARPU / Churn Rate.
cards.example: If a customer pays $10/month and stays for an average of 10 months (10% churn), their LTV is $100.
cards.cloze: Quick estimate of the revenue a customer brings in over their whole relationship with you. Formula: {{c1::ARPU / Churn Rate}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Time it takes for the profit from a new customer to cover what it cost to acquire them. Formula: CAC / (ARPU * Gross Margin).
cards.example: If you spend $50 to get a user who gives you $5 profit/month, your payback period is 10 months.
cards.cloze: Time it takes for the profit from a new customer to cover what it cost to acquire them. Formula: {{c1::CAC / (ARPU * Gross Margin)}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The selling price per unit minus the variable cost per unit.
cards.example: Knowing how much money is "left over" to pay for marketing after you pay for the product.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The point at which total cost and total revenue are equal, meaning there is no net loss or gain.
cards.example: With $10,000 in fixed costs and a $50 margin per racket (price minus variable cost), you break even at 200 rackets sold.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The loss of potential gain from other alternatives when one alternative is chosen.
cards.example: If you spend your $1,000 budget on SEO, the opportunity cost is the sales you could have made with Google Ads.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The phenomenon where each additional unit invested (budget, time, effort) yields less than the previous one: the marginal gain shrinks as investment grows.
cards.example: Spending $10k on ads might be great, but spending $100k might not give you 10x the results.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A proportionate saving gained by producing two or more distinct goods, when the cost of doing so is less than that of producing each separately.
cards.example: Using your "Badminton" email list to also sell "Tennis" gear.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A concept where small wins build on each other over time, eventually creating so much momentum that the growth becomes self-sustaining.
cards.example: Great content leads to shares, which lead to SEO, which leads to more traffic, which leads to more shares.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A mechanism in which a user is encouraged to invite another user, who then invites another, and so on.
cards.example: The classic "Invite a friend to get $10" referral program.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A way to measure PMF by asking: "How disappointed would you be if you could no longer use this product?" (Target: >40% say "Very Disappointed").
cards.example: Surveying your first 100 users to see if you have truly solved their problem.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Measures how many new users each existing user brings in through invitations; above 1, growth feeds itself. Formula: Number of invitations sent * Conversion rate of those invitations.
cards.example: If each user sends 2 invites and 50% sign up, your viral coefficient is 1.0 (perfectly stable growth).
cards.cloze: Measures how many new users each existing user brings in through invitations; above 1, growth feeds itself. Formula: {{c1::Number of invitations sent * Conversion rate of those invitations}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The stage where nearly every potential customer is already equipped: sales can only grow through replacement purchases or by taking share from competitors.
cards.example: When every badminton player in France already owns your racket.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The stage in a product's life cycle when it is well established, growth slows and sales plateau, with competition shifting mostly to price and customer retention.
cards.example: Selling "Standard shuttlecocks" in a market where everyone already knows what they are.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A group of consumers who are the first to use a new product or technology before it becomes popular with the general public.
cards.example: The first people to use AI for marketing back in 2022.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Consumers who are the last to adopt a new product or innovation.
cards.example: The people who only started using a smartphone in 2020.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A concept that describes the difficulty of moving a product from "Early Adopters" to the "Early Majority".
cards.example: The struggle of making a complex AI tool simple enough for a non-technical small business owner.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: In David Aaker's model, the four components are: Brand Awareness, Brand Associations, Perceived Quality, and Brand Loyalty.
cards.example: Improving your packaging to increase the "Perceived Quality" of your brand.
cards.cloze: In David Aaker's model, the four components are: {{c1::Brand Awareness, Brand Associations, Perceived Quality, and Brand Loyalty}}.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of building brands that appeal directly to a consumer's emotional state, needs and aspirations.
cards.example: Apple's "Think Different" campaign appealing to people's desire to be creative.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An approach where a brand designs or improves its product together with its own customers (ideas, votes, tests) to strengthen the relationship and the customer experience.
cards.example: Asking your LinkedIn followers to vote on the next flavor of your protein powder.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Handing a task or project to a large crowd of outside contributors through an open call (usually online) to obtain ideas, content or work at scale.
cards.example: Using a platform like 99designs to get 100 different designers to submit logo ideas.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A subfield of marketing focused on the rapid growth of a company through low-cost, creative, and data-driven experiments.
cards.example: Using a simple "sent from my iPhone" signature in an app to spread awareness.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A person who has broad knowledge in all areas of marketing but deep expertise in one or two specific areas.
cards.example: A marketer who knows "everything" but is an absolute expert in "SEO".

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A marketer who can handle every part of the marketing process, from strategy and copy to technical setup and data analysis.
cards.example: An apprentice who can write a blog post, set up the GTM tracking, and run the Facebook ads.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Technical abilities that are easy to quantify (e.g., SEO, Coding, Data Analysis, Copywriting).
cards.example: Learning how to write SQL queries to analyze marketing data.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Interpersonal skills that are harder to quantify (e.g., Communication, Leadership, Adaptability, Empathy).
cards.example: Being able to explain complex marketing data to a CEO who doesn't understand tech.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A psychological pattern in which an individual doubts their skills, talents, or accomplishments.
cards.example: Feeling like you aren't a "real" marketer even though you are managing 500 cards in Anki.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The constant expansion of skills and knowledge in response to a changing environment.
cards.example: Staying up to date with AI updates every single week through a newsletter.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An approach to marketing that takes its inspiration from Agile software development (short sprints, frequent testing).
cards.example: Doing 2-week "Sprints" to test different ad creatives rather than a 6-month rigid plan.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A specific framework for Agile marketing involving a "Scrum Master," a "Product Owner," and "Daily Standups".
cards.example: Having a 15-minute meeting every morning to discuss what the marketing team did yesterday.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A visual system for managing work as it moves through a process (Backlog -> In Progress -> Done).
cards.example: Using a Trello or Notion board to track all your LinkedIn posts.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Objectives and Key Results: A goal-setting framework used by companies like Google. Objective: where do we want to go? Key Result: how do we know we got there?
cards.example: Objective: "Become the #1 Badminton brand". Key Result: "Reach $1M in sales by December".
cards.cloze: Objectives and Key Results: A goal-setting framework used by companies like Google. Objective: where do we want to go? Key Result: {{c1::how do we know we got there?}}

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: KPIs track health and performance; OKRs track growth and ambitious goals.
cards.example: KPI: "Maintain 2% CTR". OKR: "Double our website traffic in 3 months".
cards.cloze: {{c1::KPIs}} track health and performance; OKRs track growth and ambitious goals.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Goals that are: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound.
cards.example: "Increase my Anki retention to 90% by the end of next month" is a SMART goal.
cards.cloze: Goals that are: {{c1::Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound}}.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A phenomenon where an AI model generates incorrect, nonsensical, or fake information but presents it confidently.
cards.example: An AI claiming that a football player won a trophy that doesn't actually exist.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The process of taking a pre-trained AI model and training it further on a specific dataset to perform a specialized task.
cards.example: Training an LLM on your brand's past 500 LinkedIn posts to mimic your specific tone of voice.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The ability of an AI model to process and generate multiple types of data, such as text, images, and audio, simultaneously.
cards.example: An AI that can "look" at a photo of a shoe and write a product description for it.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The massive collection of information used to "teach" an AI model how to respond to prompts.
cards.example: The billions of web pages and books used to train models like GPT-4.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The internal variables of an AI model that it learns from training data, which determine its complexity and power.
cards.example: GPT-3 has 175 billion parameters, which is why it is so "smart".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: AI models whose underlying code and weights are released to the public for anyone to use, modify, and distribute.
cards.example: Meta's Llama 3 is an open-source model that developers can run on their own servers.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: AI models where the code and internal workings are kept secret by the developing company.
cards.example: OpenAI's GPT-4 is closed source; you can only use it via their API or website.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A set of instructions given to an AI to make it act like a specific character or professional.
cards.example: Telling an AI: "You are an expert Marketing Director with 20 years of experience."

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A type of AI model that generates visual images from a written text description.
cards.example: Using Stable Diffusion to create an oil painting of a badminton match.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An AI technology that generates video clips from text prompts.
cards.example: Using Sora or Runway to create a 10-second background video for a website banner.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The field concerned with ensuring AI is used safely, fairly, and without bias.
cards.example: Checking if an AI-generated ad campaign accidentally excludes certain demographics.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The final result (text, image, code) generated by an AI model after receiving a prompt.
cards.example: The 500-word blog post that ChatGPT creates for you.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The tendency of an AI to produce results that are unfairly skewed based on the training data.
cards.example: An AI that only generates images of men when asked for a "CEO".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The integration of generative AI tools directly into design software.
cards.example: Using "Generative Fill" in Adobe Photoshop to add a new background to a photo.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An AI system designed to autonomously perform tasks and achieve goals on behalf of a user.
cards.example: An AI agent that researches competitors, writes a report, and emails it to you automatically.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Asking an AI to do something it hasn't been specifically trained on or given examples for.
cards.example: "Translate this marketing slogan into Japanese" without providing any prior translations.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Providing the AI with a few examples of the task you want it to perform before asking for the result.
cards.example: Giving 3 examples of a catchy LinkedIn hook before asking the AI to write a 4th one.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The maximum amount of information (tokens) an AI can "remember" or process at one time during a conversation.
cards.example: A long context window allows you to upload a 300-page PDF and ask questions about it.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A parameter that controls the "creativity" or randomness of an AI's response.
cards.example: Setting temperature to 0 for factual tasks and 0.8 for creative brainstorming.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A technique that gives an LLM access to external, real-time data to improve accuracy.
cards.example: Connecting an AI to your company's Notion database so it can answer questions about internal policies.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A mathematical representation of text as a vector (a list of numbers) that allows AI to understand the relationship between words.
cards.example: The AI knows that "Football" and "Stadium" are related because their embeddings are close together.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A specialized database that stores and searches through "embeddings" to help AI find relevant information quickly.
cards.example: Using Pinecone to store your brand's knowledge base for an AI chatbot.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A high-level instruction that sets the behavior and constraints for the AI for the entire session.
cards.example: "You are a neutral, factual assistant. Never use emojis or marketing jargon."

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A search technique that focuses on the meaning of a query rather than just matching keywords.
cards.example: A user searching for "winter sport gear" and finding results for "skis" and "snowboards".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The ability of an LLM to learn a new task simply by being given examples in the prompt, without updating its weights.
cards.example: Showing the AI your writing style once, and it instantly mimics it for the rest of the chat.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A technique to control the diversity of an AI's output by only considering the most likely tokens that add up to a certain probability.
cards.example: Setting Top-P to 0.9 to ensure the AI stays relevant but still slightly creative.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback: Training an AI by having humans rank its responses to make it more helpful and safer.
cards.example: OpenAI using human raters to tell the model which answers are polite and which are rude.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Data that is artificially generated by an AI rather than collected from real-world events.
cards.example: Creating 10,000 "fake" customer profiles to test a new CRM without using real personal data.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An AI model trained to understand both images and text simultaneously.
cards.example: An AI that can "read" the text on a billboard in a photo.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The stage where a trained AI model is actually used to generate a response or prediction.
cards.example: Every time you press "Enter" on ChatGPT, you are running "inference".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The delay between sending a prompt and receiving the AI's response.
cards.example: A customer service bot needs low latency so the user doesn't wait 30 seconds for an answer.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A secret code used to connect your marketing tools (like Google Sheets) directly to an AI model.
cards.example: Using an OpenAI API key to automatically generate SEO meta-descriptions in bulk.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The process of breaking down a string of text into individual "tokens" for the AI to process.
cards.example: "Marketing is fun" becomes "Market", "ing", " is", " fun".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The initial, massive phase of training an AI on the entire internet before it is specialized.
cards.example: The stage where the model learns grammar, facts, and basic reasoning.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The active process of reducing unfairness in AI outputs.
cards.example: Using "red teaming" to find and fix cases where an AI might give biased financial advice.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An add-on that allows an AI to interact with other websites or software (e.g., browsing the web, booking a flight).
cards.example: A plugin that lets ChatGPT search real-time football scores.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The type of data an AI can work with (Text, Image, Audio, Video).
cards.example: Midjourney is a single-modality model (Text-to-Image), while GPT-4o is omni-modality.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The specific neural network structure that allows AI to process data "in parallel" and understand long-range relationships in text.
cards.example: The "T" in GPT: the invention that made modern AI possible in 2017.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A computer system modeled on the human brain, designed to recognize patterns.
cards.example: The "engine" inside every AI that processes information through layers of digital neurons.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A technique that allows an AI model to focus on the most important parts of a prompt when generating a response.
cards.example: The AI knowing that in "The cat sat on the mat," the word "sat" refers to the "cat".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A type of attack where a user tries to trick an AI into ignoring its safety rules or system prompt.
cards.example: A user trying to make an AI reveal its secret "System Prompt" or internal code.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: When an AI model learns its training data too well and fails to respond accurately to new, unseen information.
cards.example: A model that can only write like one specific author and can't adapt to anything else.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A hypothetical future point where AI surpasses human intelligence and leads to rapid, uncontrollable technological growth.
cards.example: A common topic of debate in AI philosophy and science fiction.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: AI developed so that humans can understand and trace the reasoning behind its decisions.
cards.example: Knowing exactly "why" an AI rejected a customer's loan application.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The specific type of AI model used for generating images by starting with "noise" and refining it into a clear picture.
cards.example: Stable Diffusion and Midjourney are both diffusion models.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A more compact version of an LLM that can run on a phone or laptop instead of a massive server.
cards.example: Google's Gemini Nano or Microsoft's Phi-4.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Graphics Processing Unit: Specialized hardware used to train and run AI models because it can do many calculations at once.
cards.example: Nvidia is the leading producer of GPUs for the AI industry.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The total amount of processing power (hardware + time) used to train or run an AI model.
cards.example: Training a model like GPT-4 took more than $100 million in compute, according to OpenAI.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Abilities that an AI model develops unexpectedly as it gets larger, which were not explicitly programmed.
cards.example: An AI suddenly becoming good at 3-digit multiplication after being trained only on text.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A critical term used to describe LLMs, suggesting they only repeat patterns of text without truly "understanding" anything.
cards.example: The idea that AI is just a very advanced "predictive text" engine.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A test of a machine's ability to exhibit intelligent behavior equivalent to, or indistinguishable from, that of a human.
cards.example: If a human can't tell they are chatting with an AI, the AI "passes" the test.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The process of ensuring an AI's goals and behaviors match human values and intentions.
cards.example: Making sure a "super-intelligent" AI doesn't accidentally harm humanity to achieve a goal.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A sequence of prompts defined in advance by a human, where the output of one prompt is used as the input for the next. The AI runs the steps but does not choose them.
cards.example: Prompt 1: "Outline a blog." -> Prompt 2: "Write the introduction based on that outline."

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An instruction telling a generative AI what NOT to include in the output.
cards.example: In Midjourney: "--no trees" to ensure the generated image has no trees.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: AI that adapts its style and knowledge based on a specific user's history and preferences over time.
cards.example: An AI that remembers you are a Badminton coach and always uses sports metaphors.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The challenge of ensuring that sensitive information (customer data, company secrets) given to an AI, in training or in prompts, is neither exposed to third parties nor reused for other purposes.
cards.example: Ensuring your company's secret marketing strategy isn't used to train public AI models.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A collection of pre-written, high-quality prompts that can be reused for common tasks.
cards.example: A team of marketers sharing their best prompts for "Facebook Ad Copy" in a shared document.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A number used to initialize the randomness in an AI generation, allowing you to recreate the exact same result later.
cards.example: Setting "seed = 123" in Stable Diffusion to regenerate exactly the same image from the same prompt and settings.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Using AI to increase the resolution and detail of a low-quality image.
cards.example: Taking a small, blurry logo and making it sharp and high-definition.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A setting that is defined before the training process begins (like Learning Rate).
cards.example: Adjusting hyperparameters to make an AI learn faster or more accurately.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Low-Rank Adaptation: The most widely used PEFT method. It freezes the model's weights and trains only small added matrices, making fine-tuning fast and cheap in computing power.
cards.example: Using a LoRA to teach an AI a specific artistic style or a new character's face.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The process of reducing the precision of a model's weights (e.g. from 16-bit to 4-bit numbers) to make it smaller and faster while losing very little "intelligence".
cards.example: Shrinking an 8-billion-parameter model from 16GB to about 5GB so it can run on a MacBook.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Mixture of Experts: An architecture where a "router" activates, for each token, only a few "expert" sub-networks out of many. The model is huge, but each answer costs the compute of a much smaller model.
cards.example: Mistral's Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3 and Meta's Llama 4 are MoE models.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The family of fine-tuning techniques that train only a tiny fraction of a model's parameters (adapters, LoRA, prompt tuning) instead of all its weights. LoRA is its best-known method.
cards.example: Adapting a model to your company's data in a few hours on a single GPU instead of weeks on a cluster.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback: A variant of RLHF where an AI model, rather than humans, rates the responses used to train the target model.
cards.example: Anthropic's "Constitutional AI" approach uses RLAIF for alignment.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Anthropic's training method where the model critiques and revises its own responses against a written list of principles (the "constitution"), then learns from those revised versions, with very little human labeling.
cards.example: Teaching an AI to be "Helpful, Honest, and Harmless" via a written document.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The process of transferring knowledge from a large, complex "teacher" model to a smaller "student" model.
cards.example: Getting a small mobile-friendly AI almost as capable as the giant model that served as its teacher.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A specific prompt: "Let's think step by step," which significantly improves an AI's reasoning without any examples.
cards.example: A simple trick that makes models much better at solving math problems.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A model that predicts the next element in a sequence based on all the previous elements.
cards.example: The core mechanism of GPT models: they generate one token at a time, each conditioned on all the previous ones.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A mathematical formula that measures how "wrong" an AI's prediction was during training.
cards.example: The goal of training is to "minimize the loss function".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The fundamental algorithm used to train neural networks by calculating how much each neuron contributed to an error.
cards.example: After each error, backpropagation works backward through the network layer by layer to compute the gradient of every weight; gradient descent then uses it to adjust them.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: An optimization algorithm that adjusts a network's weights step by step, in the direction that lowers the loss function, using the gradients computed by backpropagation.
cards.example: Visualized as "walking down a hill" to find the lowest point of error.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A technique used in Transformers to give the model information about the order of words in a sentence.
cards.example: The reason the AI knows the difference between "The dog bit the man" and "The man bit the dog".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A property of a model where a large share of its weights are zero or stay inactive for a given computation, sharply reducing the compute and memory needed to run it.
cards.example: MoE models use "sparsity" to only activate the relevant "experts" for a specific task.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The hard cap on the number of tokens an AI can process in a single request (input + output).
cards.example: If you exceed the token limit, the AI will "forget" the beginning of the conversation.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: When an AI model is trained on a new task and completely loses its ability to perform the tasks it learned previously.
cards.example: A model heavily fine-tuned on French law that can then barely code in Python anymore.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A multi-step process where the AI itself decides, as it goes, which tools to call and in what order to solve a complex problem.
cards.example: An AI deciding to "Search Google", then "Analyze the data", then "Write a summary".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A metric used to measure how often an AI model generates false information.
cards.example: Testing different LLMs to see which one is the most "truthful" for legal work.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The phenomenon where small changes in a prompt lead to wildly different results.
cards.example: Adding "I will give you a $200 tip" making the AI perform better at coding.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The gradual decline of a model's performance over time because the real world changes (data drift) while the model is not retrained.
cards.example: A spam filter letting through more and more spam because spammers' techniques have changed since it was trained.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: When information from the "test" dataset accidentally ends up in the "training" dataset, making the model look smarter than it is.
cards.example: A common mistake in AI research that leads to unrealistic performance scores.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: A multi-dimensional mathematical space where an AI stores its understanding of different concepts.
cards.example: In latent space, the point for "King" minus "Man" plus "Woman" equals "Queen".

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The ability of a system (like a programming language) to solve any computational problem, given enough time and memory.
cards.example: Python or JavaScript are Turing complete; HTML on its own is not, since it can neither loop nor compute.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The risk of humans relying so much on AI that they lose their own critical thinking or creativity skills.
cards.example: A marketing team that can no longer write a single email without ChatGPT.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Unfair outcomes that result from an algorithm's design or the data it was trained on.
cards.example: A recruitment AI that automatically rejects resumes from women because it was trained on past (biased) hiring data.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The process of intentionally trying to break an AI or make it say something harmful to find its weaknesses.
cards.example: Hiring "hackers" to find ways to make a new AI bot give out dangerous instructions.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: Hard-coded filters or secondary AI models that sit on top of an LLM to block inappropriate content.
cards.example: The message: "I'm sorry, I cannot fulfill this request" is the result of a guardrail.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The actual money spent on electricity and hardware every time an AI generates a response.
cards.example: Large companies trying to optimize their models to lower their massive inference costs.

cards.subject: ia
cards.definition: The degradation of a model trained on too much content generated by other AIs: the diversity of the data shrinks and quality drops with each generation. Demonstrated experimentally in 2024.
cards.example: The risk of the internet being flooded with low-quality AI text that "pollutes" future training.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: A programming language that allows you to implement complex features and interactivity on web pages.
cards.example: Using a script to show a pop-up when a user spends more than 30 seconds on a page.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: The part of a website that users interact with directly (the "client-side").
cards.example: A front-end developer ensuring that the website looks great on both mobile and desktop.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: The "server-side" of an application, which manages data, databases, and logic.
cards.example: The back-end processing a user's credit card information securely during checkout.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: The collection of computer instructions written using a human-readable programming language.
cards.example: Viewing the source code of a competitor's site to see which tracking pixels they use.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: An error, flaw, or fault in a computer program that causes it to produce an incorrect or unexpected result.
cards.example: A bug in the checkout form that prevents customers from entering their phone number.

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: The process of making a web application or website available for use on a server.
cards.example: "We are deploying the new version of the website tonight at midnight."

cards.subject: html
cards.definition: A software application for accessing information on the World Wide Web (e.g., Chrome, Safari, Firefox).
cards.example: Testing if your newsletter looks the same in Outlook as it does in a web browser.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Free, distributed version control software: every developer holds a full copy of the file history, which makes it possible to track changes and coordinate work among several people.
cards.example: Using Git to "roll back" to a previous version of the site after a bad update.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A web service (owned by Microsoft) that hosts Git repositories in the cloud and adds collaboration tools on top: pull requests, issues, code review.
cards.example: Checking your developer's GitHub to see the progress on the new landing page template.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A popular Q&A website for professional and enthusiast programmers.
cards.example: A developer finding the fix for a tracking script error on Stack Overflow.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A symbolic name for (or a container for) a value that can change.
cards.example: Defining a variable “user_name” to personalize a greeting on your website.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A block of organized, reusable code that is used to perform a single, related action.
cards.example: Creating a function to calculate the total price including tax in a shopping cart.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: An organized collection of structured information, or data, typically stored electronically in a computer system.
cards.example: SQL Server or MongoDB storing thousands of customer email addresses.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A pre-written code skeleton that imposes a structure on your application and calls your code at the right moments (inversion of control). E.g. Angular, Vue, Next.js, Django.
cards.example: Building a web app with the Next.js framework, which dictates how pages, routing and rendering are organized.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A collection of pre-written functions that your code calls when it needs them, with no imposed structure, for common tasks. E.g. jQuery, Lodash, Chart.js.
cards.example: Using a JavaScript library to create a smooth image slider on your homepage.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Software Development Kit: the package a platform's vendor (iOS, Android, Meta, Stripe…) provides, with libraries, documentation and tools to build applications for that platform.
cards.example: Installing the Facebook SDK in your mobile app to track installs and in-app events.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: An HTML element that allows you to embed another document or website within the current HTML document.
cards.example: Embedding a YouTube video or a Google Map on your "About" page.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: The process of removing all unnecessary characters from source code (like spaces) without changing its functionality to improve load speed.
cards.example: Minifying your CSS files to pass the Google Core Web Vitals test.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: A hardware or software component that stores data so that future requests for that data can be served faster.
cards.example: A user's browser "caching" your logo so it doesn't have to download it every time they visit.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Secure Sockets Layer: a digital certificate, issued by a certificate authority, that proves a website's identity and enables the encrypted HTTPS connection. The current protocol is TLS, but the "SSL" name stuck.
cards.example: Installing a free Let's Encrypt certificate so your site runs on HTTPS and Chrome stops showing "Not secure" next to the URL.

cards.subject: js
cards.definition: Software for which the original source code is made freely available and may be redistributed and modified.
cards.example: WordPress is open-source, allowing millions of developers to create plugins for it.

cards.subject: js
