cards.example: A diagram showing that one "Customer" can have many "Orders," but each "Order" belongs to only one "Customer."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A new type of data storage that combines the flexibility of raw data (Data Lake) with the organization of a structured database (Data Warehouse).
cards.example: Using one system to store raw video files and structured sales tables at the same time for your AI to analyze.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A machine learning technique that trains an algorithm across multiple decentralized devices or servers without exchanging the raw data.
cards.example: An AI learning how people use an app on their phones without ever seeing the private data of those people.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advanced A/B testing method where the system automatically sends more traffic to the "winning" version while the test is still running.
cards.example: If Headline A is performing much better than Headline B, the system starts showing Headline A to 90% of people automatically.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical method used to find "hidden" groups or segments within a larger population based on their behavior.
cards.example: Discovering that you have a segment of "Silent Fans" who read every email but never click or comment.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of simplifying complex data sets by reducing the number of variables, while still keeping the most important information.
cards.example: Turning 50 different customer metrics into 3 simple "scores" to make it easier to understand their behavior.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A technique used by APIs to divide a large set of data into smaller, manageable "pages" so the system doesn't crash.
cards.example: Downloading your first 100 leads, then asking the API for the "next page" to get the next 100.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Running an experiment where the different versions of a page are chosen by your server before the website is even sent to the user.
cards.example: Testing two different pricing models where the user never sees the "flicker" of the page changing in their browser.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Using complex math formulas (Calculated Fields) and data blending to create interactive marketing dashboards.
cards.example: Combining your Facebook spend and Google spend into one single "Total Marketing Cost" metric in your report.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Using code (like Python) to automatically find and analyze thousands of search terms to find new content ideas.
cards.example: Running a script that finds all the "How to..." questions people are asking about badminton on Google.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A way of representing knowledge in the form of "Subject-Predicate-Object" so computers can understand relationships.
cards.example: "Théo (Subject) - teaches (Predicate) - Marketing (Object)."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The automated process of extracting data from websites for research or competitive analysis.
cards.example: Using a tool to automatically gather all the prices of rackets from 10 different competitor websites every day.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The direct revenues and costs of a business model expressed on a per-unit basis (per customer).
cards.example: Working out that a subscriber costs you 40 euros to acquire (CAC) and brings 120 euros of margin over their lifetime (LTV): an LTV/CAC ratio of 3, so the model is profitable per customer.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The cost to acquire the next additional customer. It helps determine if you can afford to scale your budget further.
cards.example: Realizing that while your average CAC is 20, getting more customers now costs 45 each because you exhausted your best audience.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A branch of statistics that helps determine if a marketing action actually caused a specific result, rather than a coincidence.
cards.example: Proving that a celebrity post actually caused a sales spike, rather than the spike happening because it was a holiday.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A quasi-experimental method that measures a campaign's effect by comparing how an exposed group changes over time versus an unexposed control group, without random assignment of individuals (often geographic areas).
cards.example: Launching ads in Paris but not in Lyon, then comparing the growth difference between the two cities.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Predictive modeling that estimates, for each customer, the incremental effect of a marketing action: their probability of buying with versus without the message. It isolates the "persuadables" you should target first.
cards.example: Targeting only persuadable users with a discount, instead of wasting money on people who were going to buy anyway.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of linking multiple identifiers like email and device ID from various platforms to a single, unique customer profile.
cards.example: Recognizing that the person who clicked an ad on a phone is the same person who just logged into your site on a laptop.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method of linking user identities based on high-probability patterns like IP address and location rather than a 100% certain ID.
cards.example: Assuming two devices belong to the same person because they are always in the same house and use the same browser.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Linking user identities using 100% certain data, like a hashed email address or a unique login ID.
cards.example: Connecting a user's behavior across devices because they logged into their account on both their phone and computer.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Google's Privacy Sandbox API (formerly FLEDGE) for remarketing: interest groups are stored in the browser and the ad auction runs on the device, with no identifier shared with advertisers. Google announced its retirement in late 2025.
cards.example: Your browser remembering you liked sports gear and letting an ad auction happen locally on your device for privacy.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Sophisticated Invalid Traffic. Ad fraud generated by bots designed to look exactly like real human behavior.
cards.example: A bot net that watches videos and clicks buttons on a schedule to steal your budget without being detected.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy to ensure ads appear in contexts that specifically align with a brand's values, going beyond simple safety.
cards.example: A luxury brand refusing to show ads on cheap discount sites, even if they are safe, to protect its premium image.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advertising business set up by a retailer that allows brands to show ads to shoppers on the retailer's own site.
cards.example: A racket brand paying a major online store to show their ad at the top of the search results for badminton.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The share of Google searches for your brand among all brand searches in your category (you plus your competitors). An awareness indicator that often leads market share.
cards.example: If the marketing coaches in your category get 10,000 brand searches a month in total and your name accounts for 2,000 of them, your Share of Search is 20%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A principle stating that the more choices a user has, the longer it will take them to make a decision.
cards.example: Limiting your website navigation to 4 items instead of 12 to help visitors find what they need faster.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A model predicting that the time to move to a target depends on the distance to and the size of the target.
cards.example: Making your Buy Now button huge and placing it where the user's thumb naturally rests on a screen.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of examining raw files from a web server to see how search engine bots and users interact with a site.
cards.example: Reading logs to discover that Google is wasting time scanning old, useless pages instead of your new blog posts.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A server setup where you intercept requests to modify content like SEO tags before it reaches the user or Google.
cards.example: Using a tool to add technical SEO data to a website that is normally very difficult for developers to change.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Moving data processing closer to the user to reduce latency and allow for instant personalization.
cards.example: A website that instantly changes its language to French based on the user's city before the page even finishes loading.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy where a company builds its tech by connecting specialized tools via APIs rather than using one all-in-one suite.
cards.example: Using one specific tool for email, another for CRM, and another for data, making them all talk to each other.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A framework that allows data analysts to transform, test, and document data in a data warehouse using SQL.
cards.example: Writing dbt models that clean your raw ad data every morning and turn it into clean, tested tables ready for your dashboard.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The traceability of a piece of data: where it comes from, which transformations it went through and which reports it ends up in. Often shown as a map, it lets you audit every number on a dashboard.
cards.example: Being able to prove exactly where a Sale number came from before it reached the CEO's final report.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A search method that turns the query and documents into embeddings (numeric vectors of meaning) and returns the closest content, even with no keyword in common. It is the retrieval building block of RAG pipelines.
cards.example: A user searches for marketing help for people who hate selling and your site finds Empathy-based growth using AI.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy that uses AI to determine the most effective marketing action to take for a specific user at that exact moment.
cards.example: The system deciding that for User A, the best move is a video, but for User B, it's a 10% discount code.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A separate, secure storage system where all sensitive customer data is kept, isolated from the rest of the tech stack.
cards.example: Keeping real names in a vault and giving the marketing team only fake IDs to analyze behavior safely.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A mathematical system for sharing information about a group while withholding information about individuals.
cards.example: A platform telling you 1,000 people liked your ad while adding noise so you can't identify any single person.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A data mining technique used to find purchase patterns by identifying which products are frequently bought together.
cards.example: Discovering that people who buy rackets also buy grip tape 85% of the time, so you create a bundle offer.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The probability, computed by a predictive model from past behavior, that a given customer will cancel or stop using your service in the near future. A statistical score, not a hand-built composite indicator.
cards.example: Your CRM flagging a user who hasn't opened your last 3 emails as High Churn Risk to trigger a reminder.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Marketing Return on Assets. A ratio comparing the profit generated by marketing to the assets it relies on, including intangible ones (brand equity, customer base), rather than to spend alone as ROI does.
cards.example: Comparing the profit your brand generated this year to the value of your brand equity and customer base, rather than only to the ad budget you spent.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A system that links marketing data (source, campaign, first click) to CRM sales data and feeds the revenue actually closed back to each channel, so campaigns are judged on customers won, not just leads.
cards.example: Your CRM telling Google Ads: That person who clicked your ad 3 months ago just signed a 10,000 euro contract today.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advanced A/B testing method where an algorithm automatically shifts traffic to the winner in real-time.
cards.example: Starting a test 50/50, but as Headline A wins, the system automatically starts showing it to 90% of visitors.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Structured data markup (JSON-LD) in which your site's entities (Organization, Person, Article) are linked to each other through @id identifiers, so search engines understand how they relate.
cards.example: Adding code that tells Google: This person is the Author of this Article and the Founder of this Company.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An SEO issue where search engines are confused about which version of a page is the master copy.
cards.example: Having two versions of your homepage active, causing Google to split your SEO power between them.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Files like CSS or JS that prevent a webpage from appearing on the screen until they are fully downloaded.
cards.example: A user seeing a white screen for 4 seconds because a heavy script is loading before the main headline.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A performance metric measuring the time from when the page starts loading to when any content is rendered on screen.
cards.example: Making sure your page's logo and headline show up in under one second, well below the 1.8 s threshold Google rates as good, so the site feels fast.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A lab metric (Lighthouse) that adds up, between First Contentful Paint and interactivity, the portion of each main-thread long task beyond 50 ms: the time during which the page cannot respond to clicks.
cards.example: A user tries to click Sign up but nothing happens for 2 seconds because the site is still processing code.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An error where short windows make low-funnel ads look more effective than they actually are.
cards.example: Thinking search ads are your best channel because they get the last click, ignoring the months of branding work.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A geo-testing statistical method that combines several unexposed areas (cities, regions) with weights to rebuild what the test area would have done without the campaign, then measures the gap.
cards.example: Using data from five cities to create a Synthetic Lyon to see how your ads changed the real Lyon.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method popularized by Google's CausalImpact package: a Bayesian time-series model, trained on the pre-campaign period and control series, predicts the curve your metric would have followed without the campaign.
cards.example: Proving that your Summer Sale caused 5,000 euros in extra sales that would not have happened naturally.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of automating the movement and synchronization of customer data across dozens of different tools.
cards.example: Ensuring that when a user unsubscribes from email, they are also removed from your Facebook ad audience.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A CDP that does not copy data into its own store: it runs on your existing data warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake) to build segments and pushes them to activation tools, often through reverse ETL.
cards.example: Plugging a tool like Hightouch into your data warehouse to send the "inactive customers" segment to your email tool every morning, without duplicating the data anywhere else.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy where the ability for a tool to talk to other tools is built first, before the user interface.
cards.example: Choosing a tool because it can easily send data to your custom dashboard, rather than just for its looks.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An architecture where software is built as a collection of independent services that communicate with each other.
cards.example: Having a Rating Service and a Cart Service working together independently to power an e-commerce site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A plan focused on getting users to voluntarily share their personal preferences and intent data.
cards.example: Running a Style Quiz where users tell you exactly which colors they like so you can personalize emails.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: iROAS: return on ad spend computed only on the sales that would not have happened without the ads, measured through a holdout or geo test, rather than on all attributed sales.
cards.example: A holdout test shows that 1,000 euros of ads generated 3,000 euros of sales that would not have existed without them: an iROAS of 3, while the classic ROAS shows 8.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The total marketing spend divided by the total number of new customers acquired across all channels, paid and organic.
cards.example: Combining your LinkedIn ad spend and your organic content costs to find the true average cost of a new student.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A SaaS metric stating that a company's combined growth rate and profit margin should exceed 40%.
cards.example: If your coaching business grows 30% per year and has a 15% profit margin, your score is 45, which is excellent.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: When the expansion revenue from existing customers (upgrades) is greater than the revenue lost from customers who cancel.
cards.example: Losing 2 clients but having 5 others upgrade to your VIP program, resulting in more money than before.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A financial report that explains the changes in Annual Recurring Revenue from one period to another (New, Expansion, Churn).
cards.example: A chart showing the Board exactly why your revenue moved from 1M to 1.2M this year.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A SaaS efficiency metric: the new ARR added in a quarter, annualized, divided by the previous quarter's sales and marketing spend. Above 0.75 it is usually considered safe to invest more.
cards.example: If you spend 100,000 euros on sales and marketing in Q1 and add 25,000 euros of quarterly ARR in Q2 (100,000 euros annualized), your Magic Number is 1.0.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A startup efficiency metric: net cash burned over a period divided by the net new ARR added over the same period. Below 1 is excellent; above 2 means growth is costing too much.
cards.example: Spending 2M euros to get 1M euros in new revenue means your Burn Multiple is 2.0.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A composite indicator, often green / amber / red, that Customer Success builds by weighting product usage, engagement, support tickets and NPS to prioritize accounts at risk or ready to expand.
cards.example: Assigning a Green score to a student who watches every video and a Red score to one who hasn't logged in for 3 weeks.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical model used in marketing to predict the probability of a binary outcome, like "Will they buy or not?"
cards.example: Analyzing 50 different user traits to calculate that a 25-year-old male from Bordeaux has a 75% chance of purchasing.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A data technique used to reduce the number of variables in a dataset while keeping the most important information for segmentation.
cards.example: Turning 20 different behavior metrics into 3 simple scores to identify your most profitable "Super Users."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A machine learning method that uses many "decision trees" to provide highly accurate predictions for lead scoring or churn.
cards.example: A system that looks at thousands of past paths to predict with 95% accuracy which leads will sign a contract today.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of getting your brand or yourself recognized as an entity in Google's Knowledge Graph: structured data on your site, but also consistency across Wikidata, LinkedIn, directories and press coverage.
cards.example: Linking your name, your company, and your specific coaching topics using structured data to get a Google Knowledge Panel.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Before letting an LLM answer, the system retrieves the relevant passages from your own documents (often through vector search) and injects them into the prompt, so the answer is grounded in your sources.
cards.example: Creating a bot for your site that only answers questions using your past 200 LinkedIn posts.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A system where AI "agents" are given goals and can use tools, plan steps, and complete complex marketing tasks autonomously.
cards.example: An AI agent that notices a drop in sales, analyzes the data, creates 3 new ad variations, and submits them for your approval.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A secure environment where two companies can match their data (like a brand and a publisher) without seeing each other's private info.
cards.example: Matching your customer list with a big news site's list to see which of your buyers also read that specific news site.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A Google Privacy Sandbox API that placed the user in a few broad interest categories (Topics) computed locally by Chrome from their browsing history, as a replacement for third-party cookies. Google announced its retirement in late 2025 due to low adoption.
cards.example: Google Chrome telling an advertiser you are into "Sports" and "Marketing" without sharing your specific browsing history.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The percentage of content on a webpage or social media feed that is composed of advertisements.
cards.example: Noticing that Instagram shows 1 ad for every 3 organic posts, giving it an ad load of 25%.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The practice of buying advertising space at a low price and reselling it (or using it for high-value leads) at a higher price.
cards.example: Buying cheap traffic from a general site and sending it to a high-ticket coaching webinar that pays a massive commission.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy used by advertisers to find the most direct and cost-effective way to buy a publisher's ad inventory.
cards.example: Choosing to buy a site's ads through one specific partner because they have the lowest fees and highest transparency.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Using statistical analysis to calculate the actual financial value that your brand name adds to your business.
cards.example: Proving that people pay 50 euros extra for a racket just because it has your logo on it.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The extra sales truly caused by a campaign, measured by comparing an exposed group with a holdout group that did not see it. Sales that would have happened anyway are not counted.
cards.example: Discovering that 20% of the people who clicked your ad would have bought your course anyway via a direct search.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical method (popularized by Google's CausalImpact tool) that models your sales before a campaign to predict what they would have been without it, then measures the gap with actual results.
cards.example: Using a tool to prove that your Black Friday ads created 10,000 euros in "extra" profit that wouldn't have existed otherwise.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method from game theory that fairly distributes credit for a sale among all the marketing touchpoints a user interacted with.
cards.example: Giving exactly 12% credit to a specific LinkedIn post that a user saw 3 weeks before buying.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A system where data is shared between marketing and sales to see exactly which campaigns result in the highest actual revenue.
cards.example: Your CRM telling your ad tool that a specific lead just signed a 50,000 euro contract today.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A strategy where software is designed to "talk" to other tools via APIs before it even has a user interface.
cards.example: Choosing a new CRM specifically because it has a powerful API that can connect to your custom dashboard.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Using servers located close to the user to change website content (like prices or language) in milliseconds.
cards.example: A visitor from London seeing prices in Pounds instantly before the page even finishes loading.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A plan to get users to voluntarily declare their own preferences and intentions (quiz, survey, preference center) in exchange for value, rather than inferring them from their behavior.
cards.example: A 1-minute quiz that helps a student find their "Marketing Type" while telling you exactly what they want to learn.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The ability for a customer to purchase a product directly inside a piece of content (like a video or article) without leaving.
cards.example: Buying a pair of sneakers directly through a button on a YouTube video while watching a review.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of managing and improving your ads specifically within a retailer's ecosystem (like Amazon or Decathlon).
cards.example: Changing your product titles on Amazon to make sure you appear first when someone searches for "professional rackets."

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Search Generative Experience: the name of the Google Search Labs experiment (2023-2024) that placed an AI-generated answer at the top of the results. Renamed "AI Overviews" in 2024, it reshaped SEO.
cards.example: Searching for "How to grow on LinkedIn" and seeing a 3-paragraph AI answer at the top instead of a list of links.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Product-Led Growth. A business methodology where user acquisition, expansion, and retention are driven primarily by the product itself.
cards.example: Slack growing because people love the tool and invite their colleagues to join for free.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Sales-Led Growth. A strategy where revenue growth is driven primarily by a sales team actively reaching out to and closing customers.
cards.example: An enterprise software company hiring 50 sales reps to call big bank CEOs.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A metric that measures the total revenue generated compared to the total marketing spend across all channels.
cards.example: Generating 100,000 euros in revenue from a 20,000 euro total marketing budget (MER of 5.0).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Breaking down your customer base into groups based on their signup date to see how their behavior changes over time.
cards.example: Discovering that customers who joined in January spend twice as much as those who joined in June.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A product's viral coefficient: the average number of new users each existing user brings in (invitations sent × acceptance rate). Above 1, growth becomes self-sustaining.
cards.example: If every 10 users bring in 12 new signups on average, your K-factor is 1.2: above 1, your growth is viral.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A phenomenon where a product or service becomes more valuable as more people use it.
cards.example: LinkedIn is valuable because everyone is on it; if you were the only person on it, it would be useless.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A business model where you use the momentum of happy customers to drive referrals and repeat sales, creating a self-sustaining loop.
cards.example: Great service leads to happy clients, who give reviews, which attracts more clients, who pay for better service.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Objectives and Key Results. A goal-setting framework used by teams to define measurable goals and track their outcomes.
cards.example: Objective: Dominate the badminton market. Key Result: Achieve 20% market share by December.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A problem-solving technique that involves breaking a process down to its fundamental truths and building back up from there.
cards.example: Instead of copying a competitor, you ask: What do players actually need? and build a unique solution.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method of budgeting where every new period starts from zero, and every single expense must be justified from scratch.
cards.example: Instead of just adding 5% to last year's budget, the CMO must prove why they need every euro for 2026.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The elements other than the name itself, such as colors, the logo, a sound, a mascot or a slogan, that make customers recognize your brand instantly even when the name is not shown.
cards.example: A specific whistle sound at the start of your videos that people associate with your coaching.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The specific cues or situations that trigger a customer to think of a category and then a specific brand.
cards.example: A manager feeling overwhelmed (CEP) and immediately thinking of your AI productivity newsletter.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The probability that a buyer will notice, recognize, or think of your brand in a buying situation.
cards.example: Ensuring your brand is the first one that comes to mind when a company needs a digital marketing audit.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: How easy it is for a customer to find and buy your product or service in terms of space and time.
cards.example: Having a Buy Now button on every page of your site and accepting all major payment methods.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The classification of target accounts in Account-Based Marketing based on their value (1:1, 1:Few, 1:Many).
cards.example: Creating a custom website for Nike (Tier 1) while sending a personalized PDF to 50 other sports brands (Tier 2).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of creating awareness and interest in your products or services to build a long-term pipeline.
cards.example: Hosting a free weekly podcast that teaches people about AI without asking them to buy anything yet.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of reaching people who are already looking to buy and converting them into customers.
cards.example: Running a Google Search ad on the keyword "book badminton coach" to find people ready to pay.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The part of the customer journey that happens in untrackable places like private Slack groups, podcasts, and DMs.
cards.example: A CEO hearing about you on a podcast and then visiting your site directly; you can't track where they came from.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The ratio of useful information (signals) to useless data (noise) in your marketing analytics.
cards.example: Focusing on sales data (signal) instead of being distracted by 1,000 bot-generated likes (noise).

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A statistical approach to A/B testing that allows you to update the probability of a hypothesis as more data becomes available.
cards.example: Starting a test and becoming 90% sure that Option A is better after only 100 visitors instead of waiting for 1,000.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A study used to estimate the impact of a marketing intervention when a randomized control group is not possible.
cards.example: Comparing sales in a city where you ran radio ads to a similar city where you did not.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An advanced data strategy that tracks and credits every touchpoint across all digital and physical channels.
cards.example: Knowing that a sale was caused by a TV ad, an Instagram post, and a final visit to your store.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: An e-commerce architecture where the front-end is separated from the back-end commerce engine for maximum speed and flexibility.
cards.example: Using Shopify for the checkout but building a custom mobile app for the browsing experience.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A method of running tracking scripts on a private server rather than in the user's browser for better privacy and data quality.
cards.example: Sending conversion data to Facebook from your server so it can't be blocked by browser ad-blockers.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A company-wide plan to collect, manage and use the data your own channels observe about your customers (website, app, CRM, purchases), without depending on third-party cookies.
cards.example: Focusing on building your email list and CRM data because third-party cookies are disappearing.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Adding detail to the contact records already in your database by directly asking those contacts about their preferences or intentions, instead of buying data or guessing.
cards.example: Adding a question to your signup form: "What is your #1 marketing challenge right now?"

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A secure way for two companies to compare their data sets (like a brand and a publisher) without sharing private info.
cards.example: Seeing how many of your customers also read a specific newspaper without seeing their names.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The team and technology responsible for making marketing processes efficient, scalable, and measurable.
cards.example: The person who ensures your CRM and your Email tool talk to each other without errors.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A high-level visual plan that communicates a brand's long-term marketing goals and the steps to achieve them.
cards.example: A 12-month plan showing exactly when you will launch your newsletter, your course, and your VIP program.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of managing the expectations and communication with people who have an interest in your marketing projects.
cards.example: Presenting your marketing results to the CEO and the Finance Director to get more budget for 2027.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The process of preparing and supporting a marketing team through a major shift in technology or strategy.
cards.example: Helping your team learn how to use a new AI content tool without them feeling replaced or overwhelmed.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: A documented set of rules that ensures a brand's digital assets and data are used correctly and legally.
cards.example: A rule stating that all social media posts must be approved by the brand manager before going live.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The unique attribute that allows a company to outperform its competitors consistently over time.
cards.example: Having a private database of 50,000 high-value leads that no one else in the industry has access to.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: The amount of money you make on each single unit sold after subtracting all variable costs.
cards.example: Selling a 100 euro racket that costs you 40 euros to buy and 10 euros to ship, leaving a 50 euro unit margin.

cards.subject: marketing
cards.definition: Search Generative Experience. The former name (Labs, 2023-2024) of Google's AI-assisted search interface, now AI Overviews and AI Mode, which answers the query directly and reduces clicks on traditional links.
cards.example: Searching for "how to start a newsletter" and seeing a 3-step AI summary at the top of Google before any website links.

cards.subject: marketing
